title: Grocer-turned-lawmaker says Mamdani’s government-run stores 'might not even last a year’
description: Rep. Mike Rulli, a former grocer, warns Zohran Mamdani's government-run grocery stores will bleed red and put hundreds of small businesses out.
fullText:
A former grocer is joining the chorus of criticism against New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plan for government-run grocery stores, arguing it would harm hundreds of small businesses forced to compete with them.

"That supermarket will just bleed red the entire time it's open, from the first time you turn the key until it closes," Rep. Mike Rulli, R-Ohio, told Fox News Digital. "And I would bet the farm there's no way these grocery stores last more than five years — they might not even last a year."

Rulli grew up with his family's Ohio-based grocery store chain, Rulli Brothers, which is now run by his brothers.

Experts Scorch Mamdani's Grocery Plan As An 'Illusion' That Will Have Taxpayers Footing The Bill

Rulli said his family's small but thriving two-location business has given him an appreciation for the challenges facing small business owners in New York City, whom he argued would be harmed by competition from Mamdani's city-run stores.

"You will put hundreds of these small businesses out of business. And a lot of these businesses are owned by immigrants," Rulli said. "So I mean, I don't think the mayor could possibly have asked for a worse situation."

Ny Governor Hopeful Vows Showdown With Mamdani Over Socialist Agenda: 'I Will Stop Him'

Mamdani, the Democratic socialist mayor of New York City, unveiled a plan for government-funded grocery stores while on the campaign trail. The city has since committed $70 million to constructing one store in each of the five boroughs, with an aim to open all five by 2030.

Mamdani discussed the agreement during a recent news conference, saying, "Once a month, our five city-run grocery stores will set prices for this core set of goods at 30% below typical retail prices."

Mamdani's City Grocery Plan Could Leave Taxpayers Paying For Every Banana

While the plan has been cheered by progressives, it has been panned by business groups such as the Multicultural Business Coalition, which the New York Post reported was threatening to sue Mamdani.

Rulli, noting that grocery stores already operate on thin profit margins, said Mamdani's government shops will likely be "operating at a loss the entire time."

"When you think about the grocery industry, [it] runs on about 27% gross. That's before you pay your bills. Once you pay your bills, you're about one-and-a-quarter, one-and-half-percent net," he said.

That, he argued, would make it a drain on taxpayers as long as they remained open.

"This is the biggest mistake the mayor has made," Rulli said.

title: Older workers say Social Security is their retirement plan. Is that OK?
description: Nearly half of older workers plan to rely on Social Security in retirement, two recent surveys say. Retirement researchers are worried.
fullText:
Nearly half of older American workers expect to rely mainly on Social Security for income in retirement, according to a new report.

To many in the retirement industry, that is a worrisome statistic.

Social Security "is not meant to be your only source of income in retirement," the federal Social Security Administration cautions on its website. On average, the retirement trust fund will replace only about 40% of the money earned in working years.

Retirement experts urge Americans to fund their retirement through multiple sources: Social Security, yes, but also retirement savings, investments, other income sources and perhaps a workplace pension.

"We would not recommend that anybody rely completely on Social Security for their retirement income," said Jessica Johnston, senior strategist for economic wellbeing at the nonprofit National Council on Aging. "It's more than likely to not be sufficient."

Few younger workers think they will rely primarily on Social Security in retirement, if they think about retirement at all. As they approach retirement, however, those expectations change.

The 2026 Retirement Trend Report from NFP, a property and casualty broker and benefits consultant, shows a gradual evolution in retirement expectations as workers age.

Only 12% of workers under age 35 said they expect Social Security to be their main source of income in retirement, NFP reports. But the figure rises to 22% for workers ages 35 to 54, and to 41% for workers 55 and older.

Another retirement report, the 2026 Retirement Confidence Survey from the Employee Benefit Research Institute, shows a similar trend: As workers age, Social Security looms ever larger in their retirement plans.

Among workers ages 25-34, only 32% said they expect Social Security to be a major source of retirement income. For workers ages 55-64, the figure rises to 44%.

The EBRI report draws from surveys of more than 2,000 workers and retirees in January 2026.

Some American retirees can rely on Social Security for income and get by, retirement experts say. But nearly half? Maybe not.

"That's way too high," said  Craig Copeland, director of wealth benefits research at EBRI. "I'm talking maybe 10% could do it," he said, and "those people would not be living a good retirement."

Within the retirement planning industry, debate rages about how large a role Social Security should play in an American worker's retirement plans.

title: Woman jailed for 'relentless' abuse of victim
description: Kathryn White's victim dies four days after reporting her crimes, after months of abuse.
fullText:
A woman who waged a "relentless" campaign of abuse against her girlfriend has been jailed.

Kathryn White, 41, physically and emotionally abused her 40-year-old victim for 11 months, after the pair started a relationship in 2021.

The victim reported White's crimes when she called 999 in July 2022, Cheshire Police said, but she died four days later.

White, of Mayfield Mews in Crewe, Cheshire, was previously found guilty of engaging in coercive and controlling behaviour and was jailed for three years and six months.

The trial at Liverpool Crown Court, which lasted 19 days, heard White began isolating the victim from her family and friends at the start of the relationship.

She moved into the victim's home, forcing the latter's son to leave, detectives said.

White controlled what she wore while shaming her over her appearance and telling the victim that her family did not care enough to visit, when she was in hospital.

The woman was forced to leave her job, police said, and later transferred all the money she had to her abuser.

White also repeatedly accused her of cheating and was reported to have slapped her after she hugged a colleague.

When the woman spoke to police on 6 July 2022, she said White had physically assaulted her in a "fit of rage".

A spokesperson for Cheshire Police said she reported the offender had ripped a door from a wardrobe and threw it at the victim, before grabbing her throat and pinning her against a wall.

She told officers she was isolated from family, friends and work colleagues and had no access to her own money, social media accounts or emails, they added.

White had also threatened to take her own life if her victim tried to end the relationship, the spokesperson said.

The testimony the victim gave played a "vital part" in securing White's conviction, the force added, after Friday's hearing.

Det Sgt Thomas Vass said White had subjected her former partner to a "relentless" campaign of physical, verbal and emotional abuse.

"Through her own insecurities, she isolated the woman she was supposed to care for from her loved ones, friends and even her own son, and had complete control of any sense of personal independence she possessed," he added.

"While sadly the victim in this case is no longer with us to see White held accountable for her deplorable behaviour, I do hope the result will provide her family and friends with a sense of much-needed closure and the relief that justice has finally been secured for their loved one."

title: Grading Stefon Diggs' $12 million gamble with the Commanders
description: There's a reason Diggs stayed unsigned this long, but it wasn't his 2025 production.
fullText:
The Washington Commanders needed wide receiver help. Stefon Diggs, coming off a 1,000-yard season, remained unsigned even as training camps began across the NFL.

Thus, a logical conclusion. The veteran wideout who spent last season boosting a high profile quarterback from the draft class of 2024 will now spend this season boosting a high profile quarterback from the draft class of 2024. Per Jordan Schultz, Diggs will sign with the Commanders to give Terry McLaurin a badly needed running mate along the sideline.

The deal is a one-year contract worth up to $12 million, reported Adam Schefter.

Diggs had signed a three year, $63.5 million contract with the New England Patriots last offseason, only to be released despite one productive season for the AFC champions. Off-field drama helped the 32-year-old two-time All-Pro linger in free agency, but as camp injuries stacked up and team needs rose (especially in San Francisco), Washington was pressed into action.

Will the signing work out? Let's take a look.

Diggs is approaching his 33rd birthday, but his game is aging well. His 2025 began slowly as he worked back from a torn ACL, but he still put up roughly an 1,100-yard pace over the final 14 games of the year. His 2.41 yards per route run (YPRR) ranked eighth among qualified receivers and was a return to form after good-not-great 2023 and 2024 campaigns. He had five different 100-yard games, not quite standing up as a true WR1 but looking like one heck of a WR1b.

His 15.4 percent catch rate over expected (CROE) was a career high. His 71 yards after catch over expected (YACOE) were his best since 2022. He and Drake Maye fed off each other, helping make the second-year quarterback MVP runner-up in the process.

Now he gets to do the same with Jayden Daniels, who slumped through an injury marred 2025. Things weren't rosy when he was healthy, in large part because his receiving corps was paper thin -- especially after injuries limited Terry McLaurin to only 10 games. Deebo Samuel played well enough as the team's top target, but it was clear reinforcements were needed.

They didn't arrive before August. Coming into Wednesday, McLaurin's top lieutenant int he receiving corps was either Treylon Burks, Luke McCaffrey or third round rookie Antonio Williams. There's untapped potential there, certainly, but nothing approaching trustworthy production. (Burks, with a 41.2 passer rating when targeted last season, is much better suited in a WR3/4 role).

Thus, it makes sense to throw an incentive laden contract at a player who could fall off due to age but hasn't shown signs of decline yet. His postseason numbers dipped, but that was as much due to Maye's backslide and constant pressure than any specific lapse in his play.

Diggs is a reasonable bet as a player. As a person, well, he spent the spring embroiled in an assault case with a former employee. The veteran was found not guilty, but there's a reason why a productive player at a position of need went unsigned through July despite being healthy. He's no stranger to drama, which at one point will overshadow his impact on the field and potentially end his NFL career.

That's the wager Washington has made. Diggs can still serve as a weekly 100-yard threat. He could also flame out, either because he's about to be 33 or because of something stupid that consumes his personal life. Given the potential reward, this is a worthy risk.

This article originally appeared on For The Win: Grading Stefon Diggs' $12 million gamble with the Commanders

title: New Eagles player wanted another team, but rejection led him to Philly: ‘They wanted me’
description: Eagles player explains why he’s happy another NFL team didn't want him.
fullText:
PHILADELPHIA — Two months ago, the Eagles made an underrated move that could make them look smart this season.

Edge rusher A.J. Epenesa, who previously played six years with the Bills, signed a one-year deal with Philadelphia on June 10. Epenesa's addition made an already good pass-rush unit even deeper.

Epenesa was not supposed to join the Eagles this year. He originally agreed to a one-year deal with the Cleveland Browns in March, but two weeks later, the Browns pulled their contract offer due to medical concerns.

Then, Epenesa had to wait three more months to get signed by the Eagles.

"Cleveland was a weird situation," Epenesa said after Tuesday's practice. "But I don't necessarily want to go back and talk on that just in a weird sense. I'll just leave that in the past and just be happy that I'm not a Brown and that I'm an Eagle."

Epenesa has only missed six games in seven years, so it's unclear what the Browns were concerned about. However, last year, he dealt with foot, neck and pectoral muscle injuries and suffered a concussion.

Epenesa claimed that he feels "very healthy" heading into the 2026 season.

In 91 games for the Bills, Epenesa racked up 135 tackles and 24 sacks. He started 19 of those 91 games for Buffalo, making more of an impact as a rotational piece.

He is not a star, but Epenesa will be a solid fourth or fifth edge rusher for Philadelphia's defense and will make one of the best defensive lines in football even better.

Playing in a 3-4 defensive scheme his whole career, Epenesa is not familiar with dropping back in coverage, but he will have to succeed in that area to earn a role in Fangio's defense. So far, he's adjusting nicely.

title: Free agent wide receiver market dwindles for the Colts
description: The free agent wide receiver market for the Indianapolis Colts continues to dwindle.
fullText:
If the Indianapolis Colts were hoping to make an addition at wide receiver, the free agent market continues to dwindle.

Recently, the San Francisco 49ers signed Deebo Samuel, and on Wednesday, the Washington Commanders signed Stefon Diggs to a one-year deal worth up to $12 million.

From 2017 through 2023, Diggs recorded at least 1,000 yards every season, including surpassing 1,800 yards in 2020. He missed most of the 2024 season due to injury, but bounced back in 2025 with another 1,100-yard season.

Leading the way at this position group will be Alec Pierce -- when healthy -- and Josh Downs. That's a strong duo. However, the depth of this unit remains a major question mark.

Following the team's fifth training camp practice, ESPN's Stephen Holder said, "There are very much still a lot of questions" at this position, referencing the uncertainty around the WR3 role. Also, who ends up as the fourth, fifth, and sixth options remains to be seen as well.

From the sounds of it, Ashton Dulin and Laquon Treadwell are taking the bulk of the first-team reps with Downs in training camp. Nick Westbrook-Ikhine has flashed some playmaking potential, but that's often come with the second unit.

There hasn't been much in terms of steady practice production from this trio. The Colts don't need someone to step in and replace Michael Pittman's production, but without a steady presence at WR3, that does make defending Downs and Pierce easier for opponents, who can devote their attention to those two.

GM Chris Ballard did say before training camp that he would "consider" a veteran addition at wideout. Keenan Allen may now be the best available option for the Colts.

title: Auburn's Xavier Atkins is unbothered by preseason hype surrounding him
description: If you think Xavier Atkins is distracted by the attention he has received this preseason, think again.
fullText:
Auburn linebacker Xavier Atkins quickly made a name for himself last season by leading the SEC in tackles for loss. This season, the expectations for Atkins are greater as he finds himself on several preseason watchlists and preseason All-America teams.

With Auburn football's preseason camp getting underway this week, Atkins was available to speak to the media for the first time this season on Wednesday, where he was asked about his preseason accolades and how those have affected his mindset heading into the preseason.

Atkins says he is happy to be on a national radar, but understands that he has not secured an award yet in 2026.

"When I came in last year, I did not have preseason accolades or anything like that, so I'm just keeping my head down," Atkins said. "We all know awards aren't won in the preseason; it's what you do in the season to get what you want to get. That's why I always try to keep my even keel level down, like, just being where my feet are. But it is a great thing, though."

"Focused" is the mindset Atkins has heading into the 2026 season after recording an impressive 17 tackles for loss last season, his first as an Auburn Tiger after transferring from LSU. In addition to his first-team Preseason All-SEC nod, recognition by the Walter Camp Award and the Bronko Nagurski Award proves that Atkins will have more attention this season. Not only will Atkins work to earn a postseason award and to boost his NFL draft stock this season, but he will also work to play an instrumental part in Auburn ending the year with a winning record and an appearance in a postseason contest.

title: Hearts face daunting Lisbon task - can they keep tie alive?
description: To say it has been a difficult few months for Hearts would be the understatement of the year.  Few will give the Tynecastle club much chance of returning from Lisbon with a positive result from the Europa League qualifying trip to face Benfica and it is easy to understand why.  It has been a far from ideal start for Wouter Vrancken.
fullText:
To say it has been a difficult few months for Hearts would be the understatement of the year.

Few will give the Tynecastle club much chance of returning from Lisbon with a positive result from the Europa League qualifying trip to face Benfica and it is easy to understand why.

Eight goals conceded in three competitive matches, just one scored at the other end, and even at this early stage of the campaign an injury list that continues to grow. It has been a far from ideal start for Wouter Vrancken.

The task does not get any easier on Thursday.

Benfica may have lost defender Antonio Silva to Bournemouth, but the Portuguese giants remain packed with quality under vastly-experienced boss Marco Silva.

Goalkeeper Anatoliy Trubin is only 25 but has 29 caps for Ukraine. Greece striker Vangelis Pavlidis scored 22 goals for Benfica last season and alongside him are Heorhiy Sudakov and Jakub Kamimski, who arrived for a combined fee of around £34m, while experienced forward Rafa Silva has returned to the club from Besiktas.

For several Hearts players, walking out in front of almost 68,000 supporters at the Estadio da Luz will represent a dramatic step up from anything they experienced last season.

Defender MJ Kamson-Kamara spent last term on loan at Glentoran, where average attendances were around 2,750. Striker Amadou Ba-Sy was playing in France's third tier, while Laurent Mendy featured in England's National League.

It underlines the scale of the challenge facing Hearts.

Realistically, the priority has to be keeping the tie alive before next week's second leg at a sold-out Tynecastle.

title: Preakness moves back 8 days in bid to revive Triple Crown
description: The Preakness Stakes is moving back one week in a major attempt to preserve the relevance of horse racing’s traditional Triple Crown. The Maryland Jockey Club announced that the Preakness will move back eight days, while the Black-Eyed Susan Stakes will also be pushed back eight days and will be run on Saturday. The move…
fullText:
The Preakness Stakes is moving back one week in a major attempt to preserve the relevance of horse racing's traditional Triple Crown.

The Maryland Jockey Club announced that the Preakness will move back eight days, while the Black-Eyed Susan Stakes will also be pushed back eight days and will be run on Saturday.

The move will push the Preakness to three weeks after the Kentucky Derby, beginning in 2027.

The announcement also confirmed the Preakness's previously reported media rights extension with NBC Sports, which will last for six years. According to Sports Business Journal, the deal will see the Preakness double its media revenue from its current agreement with NBC.

"The Maryland Jockey Club is thrilled to continue its long-standing partnership with NBC Sports for the Preakness Stakes. We believe that moving the Preakness to the fourth Sunday in May and showcasing the excellent Black-Eyed Susan Stakes card on Saturday will transform the weekend for horsemen, bettors, and racing fans alike," said Maryland Jockey Club CEO Bill Knauf.

The Preakness, which has been run two weeks after the Kentucky Derby since 1950, has seen its relevance decline in recent years. In the last five years, according to SBJ, 88% of Derby runners have skipped the Preakness. NBC's audience for the Preakness hasn't eclipsed 7 million viewers since 2021, a mark the race had surpassed every year for at least the previous 20 years.

Seemingly sensing blood in the water, the NYRA, which operates the Belmont Stakes, and Churchill Downs Incorporated announced a new six-race Thoroughbred Championship Series intended to become the premier horse racing series in the United States. That announcement, which includes the Kentucky Derby and Belmont Stakes, excluded the Preakness.

This announcement from the Preakness doesn't seem to solve horse racing's problem fully. While there is now a three-week gap between the Kentucky Derby and the Preakness, there is now only a 13-day gap between the Preakness and the Belmont.

In theory, for the same reasons as before, plus the added benefit of the new Championship Series, trainers could still elect to skip the Preakness because of the short gap between races.

That could be solved if the Belmont were also moved back a week, but that would seem unlikely. The Thoroughbred Championship Series announcement suggests the Belmont is staying put, at least for now, and will run, as usual, on June 5. The announcement included that date but did not specify exact dates for the four other non-Triple Crown races.

title: Is Dana White right? Why fight sports is — and has to be — about more than just 'holy s***' moments
description: White continues to emphasize the value of 'holy s***' moments for both the UFC and his Power Slap brand. But isn't fight sports about more than just social media clips?
fullText:
A few times lately, UFC CEO Dana White has offered the same succinct description of his own job.

"I sell holy s*** moments for a living," White said on a podcast a while back. This was while extolling the virtues of Power Slap, which he insisted will one day be bigger than the UFC in part because of its consistent delivery of those moments. (More on this in a moment.)

He alluded to it again just last week, at the pre-fight press conference for the UFC Fight Night event in Belgrade, Serbia. When he was asked which fight he was most looking forward to, White first called it a "s***** question" and then eventually replied that he was simply hoping for "a few holy s*** moments on Saturday night."

The fighters did their best to deliver. Out of 14 fights on the card, 10 ended in the first round — a record for the UFC's modern era. But then, if quick finishes is all you're after, you can usually get that just by booking a series of mismatches. Take some guy who has no business being in the Octagon, throw him in against a gifted purveyor of sanctioned violence, and you'll probably get a moment or two of memorable human carnage, at least there at the end.

It's an interesting way to think about the sport, though. Moments. Not whole fights. Not personalities or individual stories or even the vaguely mathematical logic of the rankings. Just big, crazy moments that will have Joe Rogan making that face as he grabs a fistful of Jon Anik's shirt.

Maybe this is just what it takes to adapt to the social media age. Spreading the gospel of the sport means you need clips, those little bite-sized reels you can post to Instagram or TikTok, sneaking into people's algorithms whether they like it or not.

This seems to be the entire goal with the Power Slap venture. Every time it comes up, which is to say when White brings it up on podcasts and in interviews, he spotlights its success on social media. The follower count. The number of total views per month. Every time a set of eyes falls upon a short video of some Power Slapper clubbing a stationary human target, that serves as proof to White that his side quest is working.

Behold, the massive popularity of people slapping other people who just have to stand there and take it. It doesn't matter if no one can name a single Power Slap star or recall specific, what, matches? Bouts? It's a machine for moments, according to White, and moments are what he's selling.

"This will be bigger than the UFC," White told the Trigger Nometry podcast. "You don't have to train 10 years and be an incredible athlete to do it."

In other words, any jabroni off the street could show up and give you a moment. Not like this MMA thing, which requires boring stuff like discipline and skill and training and athleticism. This is even better, White said, because "you might have a whole night of [MMA] fights and not have your holy s*** moment; Power Slap is one, two, holy s***."

First of all, imagine being a professional MMA fighter, having dedicated your life to this sport and sacrificed a ton to get to the UFC level, and then hearing the boss say that the untrained, unathletic slappers are better because they create more clip-worthy moments.

But second, from a fan perspective, what do those moments really mean? What kind of staying power do they have if I don't care about the people involved or understand some larger context for the whole thing?

Think about one of the biggest moments in UFC history: Forrest Griffin vs. Stephan Bonnar at the very first finale event for "The Ultimate Fighter" back in 2005. That fight was practically nothing but 'holy s***' moments, but what elevated it to great sports drama was the story behind it. The winner got the big UFC contract. His dream would come true. So when you saw them fighting like two stray dogs battling over the last chicken wing, you understood what it meant and why it mattered.

Moments are great for highlight reels. They fit right in among the junk food content scroll on social media. But I question their ability to make someone a fan — or to hold onto them beyond the time it takes to flick their thumb in the direction of the little heart button.

The thing that makes fighting unlike any other sport is its ability to create anticipation and urgency leading to an inevitable and unpredictable payoff. Two people want the same thing. Only one can have it. They both say the prize will be theirs. Saturday night we're going to lock them in a cage and find out, whether it takes 10 seconds or 25 minutes.

The appeal goes beyond just one crazy moment. It has to. Because if not, why would I sit through an entire UFC event? Especially when I could just hang out on Instagram and wait for the 15 seconds that matter to come and find me.

title: ‘Leicester Square, please guv’: Self-driving taxis cleared for London streets ‘later this summer’
description:
Wayve Uber wins first minicab licence for autonomous cabs from TfL but vehicles will have a safety driver (at first)
The taxi app company Uber and the autonomous technology developer Wayve have been granted the first minicab licences in London allowing them to offer self-driving taxi rides to paying customers – but with a human safety driver in place, for now.
The companies said they would start trips in the UK “later this summer” before the full public launch.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Wayve Uber wins first minicab licence for autonomous cabs from TfL but vehicles will have a safety driver (at first)

The taxi app company Uber and the autonomous technology developer Wayve have been granted the first minicab licences in London allowing them to offer self-driving taxi rides to paying customers – but with a human safety driver in place, for now.

The companies said they would start trips in the UK “later this summer” before the full public launch.

The San Francisco-headquartered Uber and London-based Wayve are racing against the Google-owned Waymo and its Chinese equivalent Baidu’s Apollo Go to launch self-driving taxi services in London. Their progress is being watched closely because the British capital will be one of the first cities in the world to have American and Chinese tech firms operating on the same roads.

Uber and Wayve said more than 100,000 Londoners were on their waiting list for the self-driving taxis.

Transport for London (TfL), the capital’s licensing authority, granted 15 private hire vehicle licences to Ford Mustang Mach-E vehicles equipped with Wayve’s artificial intelligence driving software, as well as surround cameras and radar. The companies said TfL had confirmed they reached the required safety standards.

A TfL-licensed private hire driver will sit in the driver’s seat during trips to intervene if necessary, although the software is expected to control the car.

The next step, of operating the taxis without a driver, will require Uber and Wayve to seek approval via a new process, known as an automated passenger services permit, with the government’s Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency.

TfL said it would monitor the use of the vehicles, and was ready to intervene if passenger safety was compromised. A spokesperson said: “Safety is our top priority. Any new vehicle licensed to carry passengers on London’s roads must align with our Vision Zero goal of eliminating all deaths and serious injuries from collisions on London’s streets by 2041.”

Wayve, which was co-founded by the New Zealand-born Alex Kendall, has been testing its tech in London since 2018 with safety drivers. In previous demonstrations to the Guardian the car has navigated most of the obstacles of north London’s busy roads, although the safety driver was forced to intervene at one point.

Sarah Gates, Wayve’s vice-president for global affairs and assurance, said: “This licence is an important step towards giving Londoners the chance to experience autonomous driving technology.

“The responsible deployment of these vehicles will bring us safer, cleaner and quieter streets, and we’re proud to continue working alongside regulators, communities and the public as we take the next steps towards making autonomous rides a reality in the capital.”

The licence approval was not welcomed by minicab drivers, who fear the threat to their livelihood. Matthew Wright, a regional organiser for the GMB union, raised concerns about job losses, increased unemployment and liability for accidents, and said “extreme caution” was warranted from TfL.

“This is a worrying development for our private hire driver members,” he said. “We can’t go charging ahead with new technologies without considering the implications of autonomous vehicles on all parties.”

Driverless taxi services are already operating in several cities around the world, although mainly in the US and China, where most of the software developers are based. However, US companies are essentially blocked from China, and vice versa, meaning they have not had to compete directly.

Uber abandoned its own efforts to develop self-driving technology in 2020, but it is working with several partners around the world who are in turn using different systems. That includes the Chinese company WeRide, which is operating driverless taxis in Abu Dhabi, UAE.

Wayve is also working with the Japanese manufacturer Nissan on integrating its tech in private cars.

The news came as Uber reported better than expected second-quarter gross bookings of $58.02bn (£43bn), but said earnings for the next quarter would fall below Wall Street forecasts.

The company also outlined ‌plans to spend more than $10bn on autonomous vehicles over the coming years, although it did not provide a specific ‌timeline.

fullText:
'Most people don’t want pervert glasses that can film us without our consent,' said a spokesperson from activist group Everyone Hates Elon. The group has launched a series of guerilla adverts deriding non-consensual filming by the glasses as well as an email campaign encouraging people to legally object to being filmed by Meta glasses under general data protection regulations, which over 20,000 people have signed.

Rights groups have warned that the glasses threaten the right to privacy, while countries such as Germany are reportedly considering a ban.

And while Meta’s safety guidelines say smart glasses should not be used for 'harassment, infringing on privacy rights, or capturing sensitive information', women have taken to social media to share their stories of being filmed by men without their consent.

Watch as Guardian columnist and Opinion editor Kirsty Major dives into why fears of surveillance and 'creepy men' mean Meta can never convince her to love the glasses – and read more about the glasses via the link in the bio

title: Darth Vader to become a TikTok star as Disney strikes deal on short video
description:
Characters and memorable scenes from back catalogue made available to group of creator fans
The likes of Darth Vader, Spider-Man and Moana are about to become TikTok stars for the first time – at least now on an official basis – after Walt Disney struck a “first of its kind” deal with the booming short-video platform.
In an acknowledgment of the influence fan-made content now has in the entertainment industry, a select group of creators will be allowed to use characters and memorable scenes from Disney’s back catalogue.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Characters and memorable scenes from back catalogue made available to group of creator fans

The likes of Darth Vader, Spider-Man and Moana are about to become TikTok stars for the first time – at least now on an official basis – after Walt Disney struck a “first of its kind” deal with the booming short-video platform.

In an acknowledgment of the influence fan-made content now has in the entertainment industry, a select group of creators will be allowed to use characters and memorable scenes from Disney’s back catalogue.

It is the latest sign of the irresistible rise of short-form vertical video, where users consume content via their phone screens without flipping it round to watch in a wider landscape format.

Some of the creator content will be featured on Disney’s own attempt to break into vertical video, its Disney+ Verts platform, which is currently available only in the US.

It confirms the powerful status of creator “fandom” and the power of TikTok, which has surpassed 200 million US users, including about six in 10 adults under 30, according to the Pew Research Center. The platform launched internationally less than a decade ago.

The rise of short-form video and the resulting fan content means big entertainment companies have had to become more relaxed about the use of their intellectual property.

Disney said that under a US pilot, creators would be given access to “an expansive collection of thoughtfully curated” content featuring characters and stories from across Disney’s brands, including Pixar, Marvel and Star Wars.

Dawn Yang, the global head of entertainment at TikTok, said: “Creators are at the heart of everything we do at TikTok. Their creativity extends the life of films and shows into conversations that fans discover and share.

“Together with Disney, we’re bringing the authentic creator expression of the TikTok community to Disney+, inviting audiences to experience the shared creativity that makes fandom so powerful.”

It marks Disney’s latest attempt to sanction the use of its characters by a high-profile third party, after a short-lived arrangement that allowed OpenAI’s Sora video-generation tool to use figures from its back catalogue.

The decision, announced late last year, was controversial in Hollywood, given that Sora was seen as posing a threat to some in the creative industry, and longstanding issues around protecting copyright.

Just a few months later, OpenAI abruptly closed down Sora after a backlash over some of the violent and racist content produced using the tool, as well as deepfakes and misinformation. The closure was also seen as part of OpenAI’s attempts to streamline its operations before taking the company public.

Disney’s announcement came as it revealed that the success of Toy Story 5 had helped it beat earnings forecasts. Its shares jumped 4.6% ⁠in premarket trading.

Revenues from its parks and experiences were up 10% from a year ago, helped by a 4% increase in visits to its theme parks. Revenues in that portion of the business reached nearly $10bn.

Rivals season 2 became the biggest original premiere in the UK and Ireland on Disney+.

title: This Isn’t About Rosebud, David Ellison
description: Zephyr...
fullText:
Antitrust law exists so that a free press and an open market never hang on the temperament of one well-meaning billionaire.

The heir to one of the largest fortunes on earth, who currently runs a billion-dollar media colossus, David Ellison has come hat in hand to New York Times readers asking for their sympathy. He would like, he shares in the op-ed, for us to understand his heart, and imagine him as the child he once was who simply loved movies, and wants only to make people feel what he felt in the dark. He’s a would-be Alfredo threading the projector in Cinema Paradiso! He’s a keeper of the flame! He also, he makes clear in the midst of this saccharine plea, a voter of both parties.

Ellison, so buffeted by billions and flatterers, embarrasses himself. He cannot imagine that the public actually cares about law, statutes, power, or really about anything except him, his politics, whether he can be “trusted” as a steward of CNN. The essay’s thesis is “it’s all about me,” which of course is part of the problem. Research on power shows that those who wield it cannot actually perceive others’ interests and minds. One researcher has compared excessive power to traumatic brain injury; and Ellison appears to be a case study.

But why did he write it? The reason Ellison is so desperate is that 12 state attorneys general, led by California’s Rob Bonta, have sued to block the Paramount–Warner Bros. Discovery merger under the Clayton Act. And days later, the Writers Guild of America followed suit, with its own case. Both are solid, textbook antitrust cases applying well-established legal standards to the merger’s competitive effects across three markets. We’re not talking about novel legal theories or untested applications of the law. Just facts: This deal would result in multiple highly concentrated markets with devastating effects for writers, movie theater owners, and consumers, to name just a few of the impacted markets. A judge granted a temporary restraining order recognizing the strength of their legal case.

Knowing this and the seriousness of these cases helps to understand this solipsistic letter. The tone is that of bewilderment. He might actually lose, which he will, because he is up against law and the public, not someone who needs more emotional connection.

Ellison knows how to manage Washington with dinner parties, like those he just threw for Donald Trump, and lobbyists. But state antitrust enforcement is a different world. It runs on statutes: law wielded by people who have to respond to the public. Ellison is reduced to writing personal essays in The New York Times because his usual tools of persuasion don’t work when state attorneys general are listening to the statutes.

And history tells us he has reason to be scared. We have seen monopolists like him, and his ilk, come before. And antitrust laws then, and now, ensure a fair playing field. May 3, 1948, Justice William Douglas wrote for a 7–1 Supreme Court that the “Big Five” studios, including Paramount, Warner Bros., and the “little three,” including Universal, Columbia, and United Artists, conspired to monopolize the film industry. The studios were ordered to completely separate film production and distribution from theater exhibition by selling off their owned cinema chains. The decision permanently prohibited anti-competitive methods like forcing theaters to buy multiple films in bundles and coordinated ticket prices. The decision opened the industry to allow for independent producers and actors, leading to an explosion of creativity.

Douglas understood, as we do now, that emotional pleas like the one Ellison penned this week are a distraction.

Industrial power should be scattered into many hands, Douglas wrote in a dissent opinion that year, “so that the fortunes of the people will not be dependent on the whim or caprice, the political prejudices, the emotional stability of a few self-appointed men.”

When he wrote that, he anticipated the howls of the Ellison elite: “The fact that they are not vicious men but respectable and social-minded is irrelevant.” His argument was later echoed by the great SCOTUS chief Earl Warren, who noted that Congress built decentralization into the statute because Congress was under risk of great concentrations of power.

Antitrust law is not about David Ellison’s Rosebud. Antitrust law exists so that a free press and an open market never hang on the temperament of one well-meaning billionaire.

title: The Top 10 TV Series Right Now, According to Streaming Data
description: If you're wondering what TV show to watch tonight, here are 10 certified bangers.
fullText:
As much as Hollywood has been wringing its hands over franchise fatigue, consider this: In July, a Spider-Man movie made $168 million at the box office in one day, and the top streaming series was a Game of Thrones spinoff.

Fortunately, if you are hungering for something original, you can still catch innovative comedy series like The Bear and Widow's Bay, or tense thrillers like FROM and Cape Fear (well, OK, that last one is a remake of a 1990 Martin Scorsese movie that was a remake of a 1962 Gregory Peck movie that was an adaptation of a book, but the point stands). Here are all of July's most-watched series, according to data from streaming information repository JustWatch.

Seems we still aren't sick of dragons and incomprehensible political intrigue: The third season of House of the Dragon, the Game of Thrones prequel based on a fake history tome by George R.R. Martin, came roaring back to the top of the streaming charts. With the season finale landing this weekend, fantasy fans will have to wait until the arrival of season two of A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms for their next Westeros fix. You can stream House of the Dragon on HBO Max.

Another book adaptation returning for a third season, Apple TV's Silo continues to track the downward spiral of the dregs of humanity, living together underground in a cavernous edifice that goes all the way down. If you've been wondering how things got so bad, this season goes back in time to reveal the source of humanity's downfall. (Unsurprisingly, humans are to blame.) You can stream Silo on Apple TV.

Across four seasons, we've watched neurotic chef Carmy (Jeremy Allen White) flame out as an elite chef, return to his humble beginnings in his family's Chicago sandwich shop, try to turn said sandwich shop into a fine dining establishment, experience ups and downs in his business and personal life, and finally, at the end of season four, quit the food industry altogether. Taking place mostly over the course of a single day, the fifth and final season explores the immediate aftermath of that monumental decision—on Carmy, and the rest of the restaurant's partners and kitchen staff. It's a fitting goodbye for one of the most lauded TV series ever. You can stream the final season of The Bear on Hulu.

This series from Apple TV has won nearly unanimous praise from both critics and audiences. It's a rare horror-comedy that manages to be genuinely scary and really funny. In the island town of Widow's Bay, literally everything is haunted, cursed, and otherwise beset with unspeakable evil, but Mayor Tom Loftis (Matthew Rhys) still really wants to bring tourism to the island. Mayor Tom is so married to his vision of Widow's Bay as the next Martha's Vineyard, he ignores the sea hags, fog monsters, and serial-killer ghosts surrounding him. The great Stephen Root plays Wyck, an old-timer who's always there to remind everyone that time is short and everyone is doomed. You can stream Widow's Bay on Apple TV+.

Based on the bestselling novel by Marissa Stapley, Apple TV's latest hit stars Anya Taylor-Joy as the titular con artist. Her name proves to be a tad ironic after her latest job goes wrong and she finds herself the prime target of both the cops and the dangerous crime boss—who also happens to be her mother-in-law. Annette Bening is clearly having a grand time playing the ruthless Priscilla Masterson, who blames Lucky for the loss of $10 million she and Priscilla's son Cary (Drew Masterson) stole—never mind that Cary eventually ran away with it. With a supporting cast that includes Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor and Timothy Olyphant, it's a fast-moving thriller with a sense of humor and an irresistible lead character. You can stream Lucky on Apple TV.

This London-set series stars the ultimate odd couple. Octavia Spencer plays Debbie, the American wife of a British politician, and Hannah Waddingham plays her good friend Judith, who happens to be a master assassin. After a hit gone wrong, Judith must go on the run to stay ahead of another assassin working against her, and to avoid running afoul of the ruthless agency (literally called The Agency) that employs her. Obviously, Debbie gets pulled along for the ride. It's a fast, tense, and funny thriller series. You can stream Ride or Die on Prime Video.

Like Max Cady in Cape Fear, the main character in I Will Find You has been imprisoned for a murder he did not commit. But unlike Max Cady, David Burroughs (Sam Worthington) doesn't set out to murder his lawyer. He was accused of killing his own son, and when he sees evidence that the boy is alive, he escapes prison to find his child. It's a modern take on The Fugitive: with the authorities on his trail, David must unravel a twisting conspiracy to clear his name and bring his child home. I Will Find You is a perfect summertime thriller. You can stream I Will Find You on Netflix.

The residents of the unnamed town at the center of FROM cannot catch a break. If it's not worms crawling around under their skin, it's the mysterious Man in Yellow stealing people's souls. Season four of this mystery-heavy show from the executive producers of Lost sees the survivors pushed to their limits as the veil between the strange town and the real world gets thinner. You can stream FROM on MGM+.

Executive-produced by Steven Spielberg and Martin Scorsese, Cape Fear is a 10-episode reimagining of a classic novel that has previously been adapted into two celebrated films. In this extended version, Amy Adams plays Anna Bowden, a defense attorney who unsuccessfully defended murder suspect Max Cady 17 years previously. Turns out he wasn't guilty, and Cady has had nearly two decades to plan his revenge against the woman he blames for putting him behind bars. Javier Bardem brings unsettling energy to the role of Cady, previously played by Robert Mitchum, Robert De Niro, and Sideshow Bob. If you like slow-burn suspense that gradually ratchets up tension, you'll like Cape Fear. You can stream Cape Fear on Apple TV+.

The spy thriller returns for its second season. Michael Fassbender plays Brandon Colby (code name Martian), a former CIA field agent who now runs operations for London Station, the agency's home office in the U.K. This season, the spy action grows more intricate, as Martian works to clear the name of his lover (Jodie Turner-Smith) while also going head-to-head with a possible double agent within the Agency's own ranks. You can stream The Agency on Paramount+ With Showtime.

title: Here's When Google Assistant Is Leaving Android
description: Google is kicking its legacy assistant off your phone very soon.
fullText:
For the longest time, Google Assistant was the bot to beat. While those of us in the Apple ecosystem have struggled to get Siri to follow our commands, Google Assistant could answer almost any query you had. It led the charge on conversational AI, which let you ask a follow-up without needing to restate the original question in full. I've never been one to rely much on assistants, but I'll admit that I've wished Siri could be a bit more like Google Assistant over the years.

Of course, Google Assistant isn't Google's assistant of choice these days. Since March of 2024, the company has let users swap out Google Assistant for Gemini, Google's flagship AI platform. Then, just one year later, the company officially replaced its popular bot with Gemini across its platforms and services. Google didn't outright kill off Google Assistant then and there; you've been able to use it if you wish, but it did say it would require Google Assistant at some point in 2025. 2025 has come and gone, and Google Assistant is still here, but that won't be the case for long.

As reported by 9to5Google, Google Assistant will officially begin shutting down on Friday, Sept. 4. The company alerted some Google Assistant users via email, letting them know that Google Assistant is being discontinued, and Gemini, "our next-generation AI-powered assistant," is now the official Android assistant. On that date, Google says it will begin removing access to Google Assistant from devices, though it may take "a few weeks to reach everyone." That means you may still have access to Google Assistant through the third week in September, though you could lose access at any point.

This Google Assistant end-of-life doesn't just apply to Android smartphones and tablets. Google says it will also revoke its legacy assistant from Wear OS watches, headphones, and Android Auto—at least when the feature is powered by the user's smartphone. Google says that "Google built-in" cars will still be able to use Google Assistant after Sept. 4.

At this time, Google TV devices and Google Home speakers and smart displays still have access to Google Assistant. However, in some cases, it seems you cannot revert back to Google Assistant if you choose to use Gemini on your device.

title: 10 Shows Like 'Ted Lasso' You Should Watch Next
description: More shows that let you root for the underdogs, whether they're playing volleyball or trying to run a small town government.
fullText:
We thought we said goodbye to lovable goof Ted Lasso back in 2023, but he's returned for a surprise fourth season on Apple TV. Jason Sudeikis is, of course, back as the title character, an American college football coach hired by Rebecca Welton (Hannah Waddingham) to coach her Richmond football club, despite his lack of experience with the sport. Having won the team in a messy divorce, she figured Ted was destined to ruin the franchise her ex-husband loved so much. Of course, we all know how that went: Ted (and the team) persevered, mostly thanks to his unrelenting good nature and belief in others. 

If you are looking for more streaming shows with the same can-do spirit, here are 10 to consider—not all of them having anything to do with sports, because in 2026, we need to take joy and inspiration wherever we can find it.

One minute, Russ Holliday (series star and co-creator Glen Powell) is the biggest name in collegiate football, with a future that couldn't be brighter. The next, he's fumbled a touchdown and shoved a fan into a wheelchair-bound cancer patient. Not great! Eight years later, he's looking for a comeback and, with shades of Mrs. Doubtfire, he reinvents himself via prosthetics and a wig as the title's Chad Powers, a charmingly naive athlete who signs on to the football team at a tiny Georgia college. It's a goofy premise, but Powell's performance sells it, and the show becomes more engaging as Russ/Chad is forced to ask himself whether this new persona is a total con, or the person he'd actually like to be. Stream Chad Powers on Hulu.

Amy Poehler stars as Leslie Knope, a can-do go-getter in the sleepy town of Pawnee, Indiana. Irrepressibly perky, she's the deputy director of the local Parks and Rec Department, with ambitions that extend to the White House. Her dream is as inspiring as it is unhinged, but she's hard not to root for—at least a little. In the best workplace comedy tradition, her office is filled with lovable oddballs: gruff libertarian Ron Swanson (Nick Offerman); cynical underachiever Tom Haverford (Aziz Ansari); and saucy Donna Meagle (Retta), whose mysterious but definitely wild personal life is only ever alluded to. It's all amiably silly, and full of characters determined to do their best, albeit with mixed results. Stream Parks and Recreation on Peacock.

Another well-loved TV celebrity stars in a lightly satirical comedy that's a bit more plot-oriented than a typical sitcom. Ted Danson plays Charles Nieuwendyk, a hapless retired professor and recent widower who listens to his daughter's plea that he find something to keep him occupied. He answers an ad from a private investigator seeking someone to go undercover by moving into a retirement community in San Francisco in hopes of discovering who's been stealing the residents' jewelry. As he comes to care about the people he's investigating (and lying to), Charlie's job only gets harder. The second season moves to a small liberal arts college, and co-stars Danson's real-life wife, Mary Steenburgen. Stream A Man on the Inside on Netflix.

Bridget Everett plays Sam Miller, a woman struggling to find her new direction after moving back to her hometown to care for her dying sister (don't worry: there's plenty of comedy in the drama, and it's not as heavy as it sounds). She's solidly middle-aged and starting over, kinda—making new friends in a familiar environment where she has to confront the past and the future alike. Luckily, her love of singing, and a community of goofy oddballs, are there to help. It's another story of a person of a certain age trying to rebuild their life following an upheaval. Stream Somebody Somewhere on HBO Max.

One of the best and most beloved anime series of the past decade-and-change happens to be a reasonably good match for Ted Lasso, even while it concerns a high school volleyball team in Japan. Shoyo Hinata is athletic, though short, and determined to play volleyball professionally—whatever his stature. He signs on to his high school club, only to learn that he's the only member of the once-mighty team. Hinata eventually recruits enough scrappy underdogs to make a go of it...but they're overwhelmingly defeated their first time out, in large part due to Tobio Kageyama, a brutal and brilliant opposing player. Hinata vows revenge, but soon finds himself and his rival on the same team. Now they all have to work together if they're to have a shot at the championship. Stream Haikyu!! on Netflix and Crunchyroll.

A fun, funny, occasionally serious dramedy (vibe-match here, even if the setting is very different), Shrinking stars Jason Segal as cognitive behavioral therapist Jimmy Laird, who's been in a depression spiral since the death of his wife a year before the show opens. When he tries to get through a workday following a night of partying, he chews out a whiny patient—which is not exactly standard procedure. But Jimmy finds himself invigorated, nonetheless, and telling people what he really thinks becomes his new thing, with mixed results. Jessica Williams plays fellow therapist Gaby Evans, perpetually upbeat despite her recent divorce, while Harrison Ford is clearly having a great time playing Jimmy's crusty boss and mentor. Michael J. Fox joined the cast for the third season, and it's been renewed for a fourth. Stream Shrinking on Apple TV.

Almost certainly inspired by Ted Lasso, this (mostly) lighthearted docu-series follows the fortunes of Wrexham A.F.C., a Welsh professional association football club that has seen better days, despite being one of the oldest clubs in the world. In 2020, it was bought by actors Rob McElhenney and Ryan Reynolds, who, despite having no particular experience with the sport (sound familiar?), were determined to revive its fortunes. The show has won eight Emmys so far, and won over audiences and critics with its inspiring tone and willingness to make fun of the occasional cluelessness of its leads. Stream Welcome to Wrexham on Hulu.

Quickly establishing itself as one of the great workplace mockumentaries, Quinta Brunson's Abbott Elementary portrays its cast of (mostly) well-meaning characters running up against an American educational system that doesn't always reward good intentions. It's another vibe match—a show about a group of goofballs doing their best in the face of overwhelming odds, and sometimes even succeeding. The 2022 Emmy win for the great Sheryl Lee Ralph became a viral moment, if only because it was so well-deserved for an actress representing an incredibly talented, brilliantly funny cast. Stream Abbott Elementary on Hulu, Disney+, and HBO Max.

The world of Rooster is a bit darker than that of Ted Lasso (this is more of a comedy-drama), but we're still playing in a similar sandbox. Greg Russo (Steve Carell) is the author of a series of popular, but critically dismissed, detective novels. Despite that, his world is falling apart around him rather precipitously in the opening episodes: He's started dating a grad student, and his already complicated relationship with his daughter grows even more so when she accidentally (kinda) burns down a house. It's a show about a likable, well-meaning character who struggles to maintain his principles and outlook when faced with a world that's more than happy to throw mud in his face. Stream Rooster on HBO Max.

A show that survived on viewer affection and critical acclaim more than ratings (at a time when such a thing was still possible), Friday Night Lights ran for five seasons without ever being a particularly big hit—but it's had an impressive afterlife. A drama about small-town high school football rather than a comedy, the show nonetheless stays positive and inspirational, even as it captures the highs and (often heartbreaking) lows of life for the kids, coaches, and families around tiny Dillon, Texas. A reboot is in the works. Stream Friday Night Lights on Prime Video and Paramount+.

title: Here's Why Microsoft Is Encouraging Users to Stay Off Public Wifi Networks
description: Hackers are targeting networks at hotels, conference centers, and airports.
fullText:
You've likely heard the warnings that public wifi can't always be trusted, and now Microsoft is giving you a good reason to avoid them. A new hacking campaign, known as CaptiveCrunch, is targeting wireless networks at hotels, conference centers, airports, and other hospitality venues in an attempt to steal credentials and compromise devices.

The warning comes from Microsoft Threat Intelligence, a group of security experts and researchers who found that Russian threat actors are using the captive portal prompts that appear when users connect to wifi to phish sensitive information and spread malware. Users are accustomed to seeing these pop-ups when logging onto public networks, so they're less likely to be suspicious.

As Malwarebytes Labs describes, hackers are able to manipulate DNS and HTTP traffic from these portals, which allows them to send users to phishing sites (and harvest login credentials and device codes), push malware via fake update and ClickFix prompts, and run machine-in-the-middle attacks to intercept and redirect traffic. Users may see a number of fake dialog boxes when connecting to hotel or airport wifi, such as a Windows Update or Windows Security window or a prompt to download a PDF viewer or disk optimization utility.

Microsoft researchers are urging travelers to assume that public and guest wireless networks at hotels, conference centers, and airports are untrustworthy. Whenever possible, users should rely on private connections, such as mobile hotspots and cellular data, instead of logging onto public wifi. If you're on a work device specifically, you should have an enterprise-managed travel router or hotspot that provides an encrypted connection to your company's infrastructure.

If you must use hotel or airport wifi, Malwarebytes Labs recommends using a VPN with a killswitch, which blocks internet traffic if your connection drops unexpectedly. Inspect login pop-ups carefully, and be wary of portal pages that ask for information beyond a room number or last name in order to connect. Use an email alias if you need to provide an address.

Never download software or browser updates, certificates, tools, or utilities through captive portals, pop-up messages, or web prompts, as these may introduce malware to your device. If you are unsure whether an update is required, go directly to the service or your system settings. (You should never be required to download anything to connect to wifi.) If you're prompted to copy code or run commands on your device, exit immediately, as this is a sign of a ClickFix attack. Anything urgent, such as a countdown timer, is also a red flag.

Finally, ensure your devices, apps, and software are up to date before you travel to patch security flaws and minimize the likelihood that you'll need to download anything while you're on the road.

title: Wrexham sign Preston captain Whiteman
description: Wrexham complete the signing of Preston North End captain Ben Whiteman on a three-year deal.
fullText:
Wrexham have completed the signing of Preston North End captain Ben Whiteman on a three-year deal, with the option of a further year.

The 30-year-old midfielder, who joins for an undisclosed fee, has made 200 Championship appearances and completed a medical with the Red Dragons on Tuesday.

Whiteman is the club's second capture of the summer transfer window following the arrival of full-back Danny Imray from Crystal Palace.

"It's an amazing feeling to be here, I'm thrilled to sign for Wrexham," he said.

"I think any Championship player at this moment in time wants to join this football club.

"Wrexham is a club that wants to get to the Premier League and so do I. So once the interest was there, it was really hard to ignore."

Whiteman was a mainstay during his five-and-a-half-year spell at North End, but has been criticised by boss Paul Heckingbottom, who said he forced a move away from Deepdale.

Heckingbottom feels the experienced midfielder crossed a line by telling club bosses that he had played his final game for Preston.

"Ben knew there was a line I didn't want him to cross and unfortunately he has," Heckingbottom told BBC Radio Lancashire.

"He's made his bed. I'm not bothered as long as I get another player."

Latest Wrexham news, analysis and fan views

Smith hungry for more after new Wrexham deal

US tour highlights Wrexham's stock higher than ever

Whiteman, a product of Manchester United's academy, played 43 times for Preston in the Championship last season as they finished 14th.

Born in Rochdale, he joined Sheffield United as a teenager and made his senior debut in 2014 before spells on loan at Mansfield Town and Doncaster Rovers.

He made his move to Doncaster permanent in 2018 and remained with Rovers, who named him captain, until 2021 when he joined Preston.

title: Palace set to sign Tomiyasu and consider March deal
description: Crystal Palace are set to sign Takehiro Tomiyasu on a free transfer following a successful trial and are considering a move for winger Solly March.
fullText:
Crystal Palace are set to sign Takehiro Tomiyasu on a free transfer following a successful trial and are considering a move for winger Solly March.

BBC Sport reported last week that Palace and defender Tomiyasu were in talks over a permanent contract that would see the Japan international return to the Premier League.

And Palace are understood to be pressing ahead with Tomiyasu's signing ahead of the new season.

A broad agreement on terms had been in place, with Palace head coach Pierre Sage tasked with deciding whether to sign the versatile 27-year-old defender.

The Eagles are also contemplating a move for March, who left Brighton at the end of last season.

March, 32, has been recommended to Palace with the potential deal discussed internally at Selhurst Park.

Sage is set to play with three central defenders next season and it is understood Tomiyasu is viewed as a potential option to play on the left side of the trio.

Tomiyasu's recent career has been plagued by knee issues and while Palace are convinced of the former Arsenal's man ability, the club want to be sure with regards to his fitness.

Upon leaving the Gunners by mutual consent last season, Tomiyasu joined Ajax where he made eight appearances for the Dutch side towards the end of the campaign before making three appearances – including two starts – for Japan at the World Cup.

Palace want to strengthen their defensive options this summer with first-choice central defender Maxence Lacroix having joined Chelsea.

Palace have an interest in a possible loan deal for Chelsea defender Josh Acheampong but as yet there are no indications that the Stamford Bridge club are prepared to sanction the 20-year-old's exit.

BBC Sport reported last week that Palace also hold a strong interest in Brest centre-back Raphael Le Guen.

title: Ryder Cup stars join Irish Open field
description: Robert MacIntyre, Patrick Reed, Francesco Molinari and Sepp Straka will play the Irish Open at the Trump International Golf Links & Hotel in Doonbeg, County Clare from 9-13 September.
fullText:
Robert MacIntyre, Patrick Reed, Francesco Molinari and Sepp Straka will play the Irish Open at the Trump International Golf Links & Hotel in Doonbeg from 9-13 September.

Defending champion Rory McIlroy and two-time major winner John Rahm are the headline attractions in a field that also contains home favourites Shane Lowry and Padraig Harrington, as well as Luke Donald, Tyrrell Hatton, and the Hojgaard brothers, Rasmus and Nicolai.

American Reed, who won the Masters in 2018, currently leads the Race to Dubai and has won twice on the DP World Tour this year.

The 36-year-old announced his departure from LIV Golf in January and is eligible to return to the PGA Tour this month.

MacIntyre, 30, has not played since finishing in a tie for 28th at the Open last month.

The Scot, ranked number 17 in the world, had said after Royal Birkdale he would be returning to the USA for the conclusion of the PGA Tour season this month before teeing it up at the PGA Championship at Wentworth and the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship.

The Irish Open takes place one week before the former of those tournaments next month.

It is expected that US President Donald Trump will attend the Irish Open as part of his visit to the Republic of Ireland.

McIlroy confirmed to defend Irish Open title

title: Warrington to face Wigan in Dublin in 2027
description: Warrington Wolves and Wigan Warriors are set to meet in Dublin in 2027 in the first Super League fixture to be played in Ireland.
fullText:
Warrington Wolves and Wigan Warriors are set to meet in Dublin in 2027 in the first Super League fixture to be played in Ireland.

The two teams will face each other at the newly refurbished Laya Arena, home of rugby union side Leinster, on Saturday, 24 April 2027.

"This is another landmark moment for our club, for Super League and for the sport of rugby league," Warrington chief executive Karl Fitzpatrick said.

"Following the success of the Las Vegas and Paris projects, and the appetite shown for taking our game to new audiences, Dublin is the perfect next destination.

"It is a world-class sporting city with a proven track record of hosting major international events and provides another outstanding opportunity to showcase our sport on the big stage."

The fixture marks the second time Warrington and Wigan have met in Dublin, having previously faced off at Shelbourne Park in 1934 - while Wigan also played against Leeds in a Charity Shield fixture in Dublin in 1995.

It also marks another milestone in Super League fixtures taking place outside of the sport's heartlands, as the pair met in the inaugural Rugby League Las Vegas event in 2025, while Wigan also faced Catalans in Paris earlier this year.

Wigan Warriors chief executive officer Kris Radlinski added: "Hopefully this will become another successful chapter in rugby league's growth story and show what can be achieved when we're prepared to think differently and be ambitious."

The 20,000 capacity Laya Arena has undergone a €52 million transformation before its reopening in August, in the lead up to the 2026 Dublin Horse Show.

Next year's fixture is primed to take place in the week before next season's Magic Weekend event, which is set to begin on Saturday, 1 May.

"Dublin has an outstanding reputation for hosting major sporting events and provides the perfect stage for two proud clubs and two passionate sets of supporters to showcase everything that makes our game special," Radlinski added.

"This is about creating an occasion that people want to be part of, whether they're lifelong supporters or discovering rugby league for the very first time."

title: Scarlets chief Daniels dismisses Ospreys merger
description: Scarlets managing director Jon Daniels also wants greater transparency from the Welsh Rugby Union as their future hangs in the balance.
fullText:
Scarlets managing director Jon Daniels has called for greater transparency from the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) as their future hangs in the balance.

Welsh rugby's governing body has outlined its plans to cut the number of professional teams from four to three by 2028, with Cardiff and Dragons set to be given licences.

That announcement has plunged Scarlets and Ospreys into doubt, with the west licence either being awarded to the Llanelli-based side or their Swansea-based rivals.

Daniels dismissed the notion that a merger between the teams - which was close, but ultimately scrapped in 2019 - is a consideration at this stage.

"There is currently no merger proposal on the table, so no, that is not an active discussion," said Daniels.

"Before we enter that phase of things, we have to collectively understand why we have to go from four to three [teams] in the first place."

Scarlets vow to remain at heart of west Wales

WRU confirms Ospreys or Scarlets will be cut

Scarlets sign Wales fly-half Anscombe from Bayonne

WRU chiefs have said the process to decide the framework for the final decision will begin in December and finish before the end of the 2026-27 campaign.

Daniels believes there is scope to continue with four Welsh regions, and would like the WRU to explain its rationale for removing a team in the west.

"From a club perspective, we feel that the decision, and the justification, for moving from four to three needs more work," Daniels added.

"I understand that there is data which has been used to come up with this decision. It hasn't been shared. We will really call for transparency in that discussion.

"These are decisions that are going to have a long-lasting effect, not just on rugby, but on communities in west Wales. I think that needs a proper airing publicly."

He added: "Our position is that before you can come out and make statements which have such an impact on people in Wales, I still feel there is a discussion and justification needed for the move to reduce the number of teams.

"Welsh rugby should be able to accommodate four teams, just as they do in Ireland and other countries.

"If there is data and evidence that we can't, then let's have the discussion about how you reduce the number of teams.

"Even then, I think we would struggle to see how that should be isolated to the west and not be a broader Welsh rugby challenge to face."

Daniels says it is Scarlets' duty to ensure the uncertainty surrounding them does not creep into their on-field performance.

Instead, he feels the WRU's current stance should unite Scarlets and wants to see everyone, players, supporters and staff, fighting for their future.

Welsh rugby's ins, outs and re-signings for 2026-27

"What we can control is how we prepare for this coming season, and we can show, both on and off the field, why Scarlets is such an integral part of Welsh rugby," Daniels added.

"The history, the heritage, the Welsh language, and also the facilities such as Parc y Scarlets. [We must] continue to develop Welsh international players as we always have done.

"If this continues, and this is how it will be, we are facing a battle. We have to be up for the fight.

"Our message is that we are here and we aim to stay here, continuing to play a key role in Welsh rugby.

"We are going to fight, and we want them [supporters] to fight with us."

title: Surrey beat Kent to go level with Foxes at the top
description: Surrey maintain their push for a home semi-final in the One-Day Cup with a 95-run win over Kent.
fullText:
Surrey went level on points with Group A leaders Leicestershire after an ultimately comfortable 95-run win over fellow in-form side Kent at The Kia Oval in the One-Day Cup.

With both sides knowing victory would take them into a share of top spot with the Foxes, a suitably keen contest ensued in the south London sunshine.

With the match reduced to 49-overs a side due to rain shortly before the scheduled start, Surrey openers Ryan Patel and Dom Sibley constructed a smooth century stand after Kent chose to bowl first.

After Patel's inevitable-looking century was cut short on 73 and Sibley removed for 53, Kent started to turn the screw.

Although Rory Burns and Ollie Sykes respectively blitzed 18-ball cameos of 33 and 28, canny bowling from Matt Milnes (3-32), Ekansh Singh (2-52) and Jaydn Denly (1-32) kept Surrey below 300 as they were bowled out for 286.

Kent, who have been in ruthless target-chasing form in their past couple of games, made a cautious start before losing their way as five wickets tumbled for 58 in under 15 overs as 30-0 became 88-5.

A near run-a-ball stand of 86 between Denly (51) and Singh (46) kept the rate required in single figures but when the pair were dismissed within three balls of each other, Kent were 174-7 and heading for defeat.

Tommy Ealham (3-37), Tom Lawes (4-40) and miserly Dan Worrell (0-18) - the latter pair released from their Hundred commitments to play - were all outstanding as Lawes cleaned up the tail to make sure Kent ultimately fell well short on 191 all out.

Abbott blast for Hampshire sinks Glamorgan

Drizzle just before play was due to start at 11:00 [BST] meant the action was delayed by 10 minutes and resulted in an over being docked off each innings.

Perhaps buoyed by successfully chasing down 294 and 314 in their past two group matches, Kent chose to stick Surrey in after winning the toss but could not take advantage of any early moisture as Patel and Sibley got the home side off to a confident start.

Left-hander Patel, in particular, looked in superb touch, lashing 13 fours and one six in collecting his fourth half-century of the competition off 54 balls as the openers put on 116.

He looked well set to convert that into a hundred but mis-hit a lofted square drive off the left-arm spin of Denly and was caught in the deep, 27 short of three figures.

That slowed their momentum, with 10 overs passing without another boundary, as Sibley was drawn into grazing a tempting leg-spinner from Matt Parkinson to wicketkeeper Chris Benjamin four balls after reaching his 50.

But skipper Burns launched a savage counter-attack, with 26 of his 33 runs coming in boundaries before he slapped Grant Stewart to extra cover.

Sykes then emulated his captain with three Row-Z sixes before a slower ball from Singh induced a skied catch to deep mid-wicket.

Josh Blake, with a measured 27-ball 32, did his best to get Surrey to 300 but when he perished to the excellent Milnes the home side's hopes of that mark fell away as they were bowled out 14 runs short.

In reply, Kent struggled to get going, managing only 33 off their opening powerplay as Ben Dawkins was brilliantly caught behind the stumps one-handed by Burns for nine as he drove on the up off Lawes.

Patel picked up the key wicket of in-form skipper Daniel Bell-Drummond for 27, as he, Sam Northeast (24) and big-hitting Chris Benjamin (0) all perished within eight overs.

Denly and Singh's entertaining effort prevented Kent from collapsing in a heap but when Denly feathered a ramp shot to Burns off Lawes, the writing was inked on the wall.

Surrey's victory means they trail the Foxes on net run rate going into the final two group games, with the side finishing top securing a home semi-final.

In Wednesday's other game in the One-Day Cup in Group B, last year's runners up Hampshire kept their hopes of reaching the knockout stages intact with a 90-run win over Glamorgan in Southampton.

title: Ex-England prop Marler to become BBC's first celebrity Gladiator
description: The former rugby star will be known as Mauler when the fourth series airs in 2027, the BBC confirmed.
fullText:
Former rugby star Joe Marler is to become the first ever celebrity Gladiator on the BBC's popular entertainment series.

The 36-year-old, who also took part in the first series of Celebrity Traitors, will be known as Mauler and face contenders when the fourth series of Gladiators begins in 2027.

"Mauler will see you now," Marler said in a video posted on Instagram, external announcing the news, recorded in the Gladiators dressing room.

The BBC said Marler will make his debut with a series of "special appearances packed with power, personality and plenty of surprises".

Filming for the fourth series is currently under way in Sheffield, the BBC confirmed in a statement.

"Known for his uncompromising style of play and larger-than-life sense of humour, Joe has built a reputation as one of the UK's most entertaining sporting personalities," the corporation said.

"Now, he's taking on an entirely new challenge as he joins the ranks of the Gladiators, bringing his trademark physicality and competitive spirit to one of television's toughest arenas."

The former England rugby international star, who is from Heathfield, Sussex, will join fellow Gladiators such as Nitro, Viper, Diamond and Sabre in battle when the show returns next year.

Gladiators was a hugely successful show on ITV in the 1990s, and saw members of the public take on a group of elite athletes who each had their own on-screen persona.

Olympic swimmer Sharron Davies, who like Marler was already known as a famous sports personality, joined that iteration of the show in 1995 as the character Amazon.

The format was revived by Sky for two series in 2008, before the current iteration launched in 2024, quickly becoming a hit for BBC One.

A celebrity spin-off is separately in the works, featuring contestants including presenter AJ Odudu, comedian Sara Pascoe, podcaster Chris Ramsey and social media star George Clarke.
