title: Why Arsenal are signing Newcastle captain Guimaraes
description: With Bruno Guimaraes set to sign for Premier League champions Arsenal, BBC Sport look at why the Gunners wanted the Newcastle skipper.
fullText:
Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta made clear in the immediate aftermath of the Gunners' Premier League title win that they would need to be ambitious to build on their success - and the club have backed him with the move to sign Newcastle captain Bruno Guimaraes.

Arsenal won the league for the first time in 22 years last season and reached the Champions League final where they were beaten by Paris St-Germain.

But as soon as the curtain came down on that campaign and the parade to celebrate their new silverware had finished, Arteta's thoughts moved to taking Arsenal to a "different dimension".

And with Brazil's Guimaraes set to be part of a new-look Arsenal midfield, the club believe they are signing a player who will do exactly that.

Arteta has always been keen on signing players with Premier League experience and who have shown they can operate with the demands at the highest level.

And with the addition of the 28-year-old, the club's aim of creating one of the best midfields in world football is a step closer.

There are a number of reasons why Guimaraes was the player Arteta decided can ensure Arsenal are ready to fight on multiple fronts.

The Gunners were plagued with injuries last season and, despite a £250m spend in the last summer transfer window, a player's robustness has always been considered when making signings.

Arsenal played 63 games in all competitions last season and have revamped their medical department before the new campaign.

Christian Norgaard, who is set to move to Everton, was brought in last summer but was not trusted by Arteta and was limited to just seven appearances and one start in the league last season.

That put heavy demands on Martin Zubimendi and Declan Rice, with the former dropping out of the side completely as the amount of work he was asked to do took its toll during the run-in.

Rice is coming back from a World Cup campaign where he helped England reach the semi-finals after a season in which he played the most minutes of any outfield player at Arsenal.

Rice has been carrying a hamstring issue but rest is expected to have helped to ease the problem, with Guimaraes' addition ensuring there will be no dip in quality if Arteta rotates his starting XI, while the ceiling of the midfield is raised too.

Arteta is known for demanding intensity in training and with Guimaraes set to join a midfield stocked with Rice, Zubimendi, captain Martin Odegaard, Eberechi Eze, Mikel Merino, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Ethan Nwaneri, there will be no shortage of competition.

Arsenal have a leadership group that supports club captain Odegaard but, with the addition of Guimaraes, they will be bringing in a player who is a natural leader.

Guimaraes became Newcastle's talisman during his time at St James' Park and, as Arteta looks to maximise every marginal gain he can, the Brazilian's ability and his way of connecting with supporters will be another weapon.

Arsenal have had campaigns seriously affected by injury, but Guimaraes has missed just 16 Premier League games since he signed for Newcastle in 2022.

And his impact is backed up by the fact Newcastle's win percentage (12.5%), points per game (0.7), average goals for (0.8) and even average goals against (1.6) all suffer in the top flight when he is not available.

Although it is an admittedly larger sample size, Opta data shows that Newcastle's win percentage (50.7%), points per game (1.7), average goals for (1.9) and average goals against (1.3) have been significantly higher when Guimaraes has featured.

Guimaraes was Newcastle's top scorer in the league last season with nine goals and he provided four assists for Brazil at the World Cup in his five starts.

Despite missing six games with hamstring injury towards the end of last season, Guimaraes still ranked in the top five players across the league for defensive line-breaking passes (46) and through balls (21).

He also led the way at Newcastle for passes under high intensity pressure (998), which illustrates how he relishes responsibility.

Staff at Newcastle have called him an "inspirational" figure and Arsenal and Arteta will be hoping he can produce the same feeling at Emirates Stadium.

title: Trump’s tariffs were supposed to boost American manufacturing, but the new levies are actually pushing some companies back to China
description: “The story that it is bringing back manufacturing is really not the story,” economist Mary Lovely warned. “Manufacturing is not coming back.”
fullText:
In both of his administrations, President Donald Trump has wielded tariffs as a means of discouraging trade relationships with China, as well as incentivizing American reshoring, but this strategy may be backfiring. As Trump's import tax plan continues to fluctuate, some U.S. companies who initially moved away from China are now reinvesting in suppliers there.

Alliance Consumer Group, a Texas-based flashlight company, encouraged its Chinese manufacturer to build a factory for its products in Thailand when U.S. tariffs on China ballooned last year, making it financially challenging to import manufactured goods from there. But now that the levies on Chinese goods have fallen to similar levels as other areas of southeast Asia such as Vietnam and Thailand, Alliance Consumer Group is reconsidering where it manufactures its flashlights.

"Have we pulled back to China? Yes, we have," Phil Laster, chief operations officer of Alliance Consumer Group, told the New York Times.

According to Mary Lovely, an economist at the Peterson Institute for International Economics (PIIE), there's other anecdotes like this one. There's not yet quantitative data on how many U.S. companies are returning to Chinese suppliers as a result of tariffs, but a trend in this direction "does make sense, given that the tariff differential between China and other countries has come down because of the invalidation of the Liberation Day tariffs," she told Fortune.

The U.S. still has levies imposed on Chinese goods, but the magnitude of the taxes have fallen from the 145% imposed on Liberation Day last April. Under Trump's recent Section 301 tariffs, China and Vietnam face a similar 12.5% tariff rate, and Cambodia, Indonesia, and Malaysia have a 10% rate.

While Trump's new batch of levies has effectively neutralized the advantage other countries have over China in exporting cheaper goods to U.S. companies, there have long been signs the tariffs have done little to curb America's reliance on China for key products like consumer goods. Moreover, the trickle of U.S. companies returning to China for those goods may be indicative of a larger phenomenon economists say is unlikely to resolve anytime soon: The U.S. is tethered to China when it comes to trade, and it means Trump's reshoring efforts will likely remain a fantasy.

"The story that it is bringing back manufacturing is really not the story," Lovely said. "Manufacturing is not coming back."

Indeed, between April and November of last year, the U.S. saw 59,000 fewer manufacturing jobs. While Trump's tariffs on China beginning in 2018 have correlated with lower rates of Chinese imports, that data point doesn't tell the whole story, Lovely argued. According to data collected by PIIE and published on Tuesday, the share of China's imports to the U.S. fell from nearly 18% in 2018 to about 11% today, but China's share of total value added in U.S. imports has remained at about 15% over the same time period.

title: Nazi warships, mammoth bones emerge as Danube River dries up
description: Water levels on the Danube River have dropped so low that dozens of World War II German battleships – and even the remains of an ancient woolly mammoth — are emerging into view.
fullText:
Water levels on the Danube River, the second longest in Europe, have dropped so low because of drought that the hulks of dozens of World War II German battleships — and even the remains of an ancient woolly mammoth — are emerging into view.

They are a curious distraction from the summer heat crisis. The Danube's record-low water levels have also forced power plants to the brink of shutting down, and governments across Central and Eastern Europe are taking steps to conserve electricity.

In the middle of the river separating Serbia and Romania, near the Serbian port of Prahovo, a rusty hull is now visible, along with a broken mast where the Nazi flag once flew.

The ships, some still laden with weapons, belonged to Nazi Germany's Black Sea fleet that the Germans deliberately sank as they retreated from Romania and as Soviet forces advanced deeper into Europe near the end of the war.

At least 20 World War II wrecks of various sizes are now visible to the naked eye from the banks of Prahovo.

Ivica Gavrilovic, who has spent his whole life living beside the Danube, said the interest in the wrecks was high but access remained difficult. "People still don't know how to access the ships themselves," he said, while taking a family of three out on his small boat.

Historians say up to 200 German warships were scuttled in September 1944 near Prahovo in the Danube gorge as they came under Soviet fire. The idea behind the deliberate sinking was to slow down the Soviet advance in the Balkans. But Nazi Germany surrendered months later, in May 1945.

The sight of the old warships is a reminder that the Serbian government, with European Union financial support, has long been trying to do something about them. Some were removed from the river by Communist Yugoslav authorities, but most have remained because of the explosives they carried.

Now, however, authorities are trying to keep traffic flowing on the Danube, which flows through 10 nations, as the dropping water levels create dangerous conditions. Experts have linked the unusually hot weather to global warming and other factors.

Krsta Brandic, a Prahovo resident, said the low water levels have almost stopped ship traffic: "As you can see, the (big) ships can't pass anymore."

The old vessels have emerged before. In 2024, a trove of sunken Nazi ships, still decked out with explosives, emerged in the Danube following a blistering summer drought. Dozens of scattered ships operated by Nazi Germany's Black Sea fleet also appeared in 2022 near Prahovo after water levels reached record lows.

Meanwhile, falling water levels in the Danube unveiled bones of a mammoth in Bulgaria, a local museum director told AFP.

The bone fragments found near the northeastern city of Ruse "very likely" belonged to a woolly mammoth that lived during the Ice Age, said Nikolay Nenov, director of the Regional Historical Museum.

Specialists have so far identified a jawbone, fragments of tusks, part of a shoulder blade, and a femur with its articular head among the stash, Nenov said.

The animal is thought to have been young and the dark color of the bones may indicate that it spent a lot of time in a marshy environment, he added.

The bones are an important discovery because they are well preserved and "unlike many previous discoveries ... were concentrated in the same place," indicating that they all belonged to the same animal, Nenov said.

Woolly mammoths coexisted with early humans who hunted the cold-resistant herbivores for food and used their tusks and bones as tools.

The animals died out about 4,000 years ago. For decades, scientists have been recovering bits and pieces of mammoth tusks, bones, teeth and hair.

title: Moss set to succeed Stevens in House after Michigan primary win
description: Michigan state Sen. Jeremy Moss (D) is projected to win the Democratic primary in the state’s 11th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Moss, the president pro tempore of the ...
fullText:
Michigan state Sen. Jeremy Moss (D) is projected to win the Democratic primary in the state's 11th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Moss, the president pro tempore of the Michigan Senate since January 2023, defeated a crowded field of five other Democrats in the primary. His victory puts him on a glide path to succeed Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), who ran in the party's primary in the race to replace retiring Michigan Sen. Gary Peters (D) on Tuesday.

In the general election, Moss will face Republican Ethan Baker, who ran unopposed in the GOP primary. Baker has been the mayor of Troy, Mich., since 2019.

Moss first entered the Michigan House in 2015, before moving over to the state Senate four years later. If elected in November, the 40-year-old would become the first openly gay member of Congress from Michigan.

Stevens has represented the 11th district since January 2019, after she defeated Republican Lena Epstein by less than 7 points in her first race. She then defeated Republican Eric Esshaki by less than 2.5 points in 2020.

But the state's independent redistricting commission redrew the district in 2021, combining areas from the previous 11th district with parts of Michigan's 9th Congressional District, according to a 2022 analysis by Michigan Public.

Over the subsequent two cycles, Stevens defeated her GOP opponents by roughly 23 points and nearly 20 points, respectively.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report (CPR) anticipates the seat will stay blue, rating it as solidly in the Democratic camp. DDHQ, meanwhile, gives Moss a 99 percent chance of winning.

On the campaign trail, Moss has touted his proposals to lower the cost of living, including healthcare expenses. He also told CBS News Detroit earlier this month he has "never been a status quo" politician despite his decade-plus tenure in the state legislature

"I think we need a stronger Democratic Party," Moss added. "I've been saying all along, we can no longer be the party that shows up to the knife fight with a pie chart."

Moss also had a clear financial edge over Baker as of the end of June, as his campaign had more than $414,000 on hand to less than $96,000 for the Republican's operation, according to the Federal Election Commission.

title: Ukraine accuses Russia of war crime after video shows drone attacking vegetable seller in Kherson
description: KYIV, Aug 4 () - Ukraine on Tuesday accused Russia of committing a war crime after a video was released showing a drone chasing down and wounding a vegetable seller in the southern Ukrainian city of K...
fullText:
KYIV, Aug 4 (Reuters) - Ukraine on Tuesday accused Russia of committing a war crime after a video was released showing a drone chasing down and wounding a vegetable seller in the southern Ukrainian city of Kherson.

Footage released by Ukrainian police ‌shows the drone pursuing a man around a van being used as a street stand before exploding as he dives for ‌cover behind the vehicle. Police said the man in his 50s survived but suffered shock and shrapnel injuries.

Ukrainian officials later identified him only as a 52-year-old called Yurii and released ​a video interview with him from a hospital ward.

"Today, many were shocked by yet another video of the drone 'safari' Russians are carrying out against civilians in Kherson," President Volodymyr Zelenskiy wrote on X, saying that "Russia has gone mad" and calling for more pressure on Moscow and strong security guarantees for Ukraine.

"We must act and support life in ways that force Russia to think seriously about peace rather than expanding the range of its drones."

Russia's Defence Ministry did not immediately respond to Reuters request for comment ⁠on the incident.

The vegetable seller went to Kherson in the morning to sell produce, said Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the Kherson regional military administration. Prokudin released the video interview with the man on the Telegram app.

"I only just put up the umbrella and started unloading the boxes. My wife was there, ​too. ​Then we heard it buzzing but could not even see it. It came ​from somewhere behind the market, from those bushes over there, ‌and flew in very low," said Yurii, sitting in a hospital ward.

"It is open steppe. There is nowhere to go. It is terrifying, of course. Really terrifying."

On the video, Yurii showed his wounds on both legs and also on his back. His wife ran off and was not injured, he said.

Sybiha said the attack formed part of a deliberate Russian campaign to intimidate civilians. "This barbaric Russian war crime in Kherson demands international condemnation and justice, but thousands of similar crimes never come to the public eye," he wrote on Telegram.

In July, the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission ‌in Ukraine said it had documented 1,396 civilian deaths and 7,978 injuries in ​the first six months of 2026, marking a 37% increase from 2025 and more than ​double the figures from 2024.

It said that the surge in ​civilian casualties was primarily driven by intensifying Russian long-range missile and drone strikes targeting cities far from the front ‌lines.

Ukraine is also attacking Russia with drones and long-range missiles, ​many of which have caused civilian ​casualties, Russian authorities say.

Russia on Monday accused Ukraine of terrorism after seven people, including three children, were killed at its Black Sea holiday resort of Gelendzhik in what it said was a deliberate Ukrainian drone attack on civilians.

A Ukrainian official said that the drone ​only fell on the beach in Gelendzhik because ‌it was shot down by Russian air defences, adding that "Ukraine uses its weapons exclusively against the Russian military-industrial complex and economic ​infrastructure facilities".

Both Russia and Ukraine deny targeting civilians in the war triggered by Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

(Reporting ​by Aleksandar Vasovic, Olena Harmash; Editing by Ros Russell and Hugh Lawson)

title: Records show rescued ‘house of horrors’ Ohio kids attended school for 2 years
description: A truancy case was dismissed after officials said they couldn't locate the parents.
fullText:
Editor's Note: This story contains discussions of child abuse that may be disturbing. Reader discretion is advised. If you suspect a child is being abused, find out how to report it in your state here. To connect with a counselor, you can call the National Child Abuse Hotline at 1-800-422-4253.

(NewsNation) — New school records show six of the 16 children rescued from a Vinton County, Ohio home this summer were enrolled in public school for two years before they stopped showing up.

The records show the six eldest Siders children were enrolled in public elementary school — the same school their mother had attended — in 2020, but were unenrolled in 2022 because they hadn't attended class for the entire 2021-2022 school year, NewsNation affiliate WCMH reported.

A truancy case for the absences was dismissed after officials said they couldn't locate the children's parents to serve them court papers.

Gary Siders Sr., 73, Christina Siders, 67, Gary Siders Jr., 36 and Elizabeth Siders, 33, were arrested June 30 and each face 16 counts of child endangerment after investigators say they found 16 children, ages 1 to 18, living in what officials described as "horrific" conditions.

The children are now in state custody. Advocates say the case's complexity could make it hard to place them together in foster care.

title: Should retirees be worried about Medicare subsidy program ending?
description: Retirees shouldn't be alarmed by the ending of a Biden-era Medicare premium subsidy program, an industry expert says.
fullText:
(NewsNation) — Retirees shouldn't be alarmed by the ending of a Biden-era Medicare premium subsidy program, an industry expert says.

Last week, the Trump administration said it would move to shutter the program, subsequently bringing to an end Medicare Part D subsidies at the cessation of 2026.

Medicare Part D is optional prescription drug coverage offered by private insurance companies to help people with Medicare pay for brand-name and generic medications.

It is available as a stand-alone plan to add to original Medicare or as part of a bundled Medicare Advantage plan.

"While headlines about the end of Medicare's premium stabilization program may sound alarming, retirees shouldn't confuse that change with a loss of Medicare prescription drug coverage," Chris Maikels, senior actuary and strategy leader of retiree solutions at Aptia Group, told NewsNation.

"Medicare Part D remains intact, and the 'Extra Help' program, which provides financial assistance with prescription drug costs for eligible lower-income Medicare beneficiaries, is not going away."

The program was restructured under former President Biden to implement a $2,000 annual cap on out-of-pocket spending on prescription drugs. It also permitted Medicare to negotiate prices for certain high-cost Part D drugs.

The majority of enrollees in the subsidy program were seniors or those with disabilities, who are now awaiting information regarding new monthly prices.

"In addition, one of the most significant consumer protections created by the Inflation Reduction Act, the annual cap on out-of-pocket prescription drug spending under Medicare Part D, remains in effect. What could change are the premiums, formularies and plan offerings available in 2027," Maikels said.

"Retirees should plan to review their options during Medicare's annual enrollment period to determine if making a change could reduce their expected costs."

NewsNation partner The Hill contributed to this report.

title: Ukraine says missile interceptor deliveries have fallen to third of 2025 level
description: Allies have supplied just a third of the air defence missiles to Ukraine in 2026 compared with 2025, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Wednesday, as Russia escalates
fullText:
KYIV, Aug 5 (Reuters) - Allies have supplied just a third of the air defence missiles to Ukraine in 2026 compared with 2025, President ‌Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Wednesday, as Russia escalates strikes on the capital ‌of Kyiv and its southern port hub.

Ukraine has been short on U.S.-made Patriot interceptors capable of ​downing Russian ballistic missiles since the start of the war. But in recent weeks, the acute shortage came into focus, with Moscow pummelling Kyiv, on average, every three days in July alone.

"And this is not just a summer phenomenon - it applies to ‌every period of the first ⁠half of 2026," Zelenskiy added on the Telegram app.

In what has become a pattern in recent weeks, Ukrainian air defences failed ⁠to intercept a single one of the 24 ballistic missiles and four Zircon cruise missiles during Wednesday's attack, the air force said.

Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukraine's president ​on the ​development of defence technology, estimates that Russia ​is capable of launching 100 ‌ballistic missiles every month to attack logistic hubs, industrial facilities, food and building warehouses.

"The war of attrition has entered its next phase," he said on the Telegram app.

In addition to its own capabilities, Russia again turned to the deployment of North Korean missiles. Last week, Moscow's troops fired the first two North Korean missiles ‌since last August, Ukraine said.

A North Korean missile ​unit has begun deploying to western Russia and ​could be equipped with 120 ​ballistic missiles and six launchers, according to Ukraine's military intelligence.

With ‌interceptor stocks limited across the globe and ​political volatility affecting ​supplies, one possible way for Ukraine to counteract is to target Russian missile launchers, some military analysts say.

Ukraine's current capabilities do not permit such strikes. ​Kyiv is also pressing ‌allies to develop a pan-European anti-ballistic system and has sought a licence ​from the U.S. to produce Patriot missiles itself.

title: 'Squad' socialist scores re-election nod as radical wave continues to sweep party
description: Rashida Tlaib's Democratic primary win extends a surge of progressive and Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidates unseating incumbents.
fullText:
Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., one of Congress' most outspoken progressives and a member of the "Squad," won the 12th Congressional District's Democratic primary Tuesday evening, teeing up her re-election for a fifth term.

Tlaib's primary victory against Michigan state lawmaker Shanelle Jackson and Inkster Mayor Byron Nolen continues a string of victories for progressives as the Democratic Party's far-left wing enjoys pronounced primary election success that has strengthened the hand of its coalition. It has also widened the range of positions held by their candidates.

When Tlaib and fellow Squad members joined the House of Representatives in 2019, their campaigns stood out for their far-left views. Tlaib and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., in particular, stood out because of their membership in the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

Eight years later, the DSA has backed Tlaib again.

Bernie Sanders, Dsa Reveal Demands For Dem Party After Socialists Sweep New York Elections

"For years, Rashida has been a strong voice in the halls of the Capitol, unapologetically standing up for the working class everywhere. Fighting for affordable housing, for clean air and water, for an end to the genocide in Gaza, and so much more – Rashida is a beacon of hope and courage for those in her district and across the world," the group said in a statement.

The group has also vastly expanded its influence beyond established figures like Tlaib.

From primary candidates in New York like socialist Darializa Avila Chevalier and her victory over incumbent Rep. Adriano Espaillat, D-N.Y., the veteran chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, to Melat Kiros, another socialist in Colorado, unseating 30-year incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette, D-Colo., progressives have expanded their influence over the party.

It's a stark reversal of the party's finger-pointing in the wake of disappointing 2020 congressional election results where Democrats were left with slimmer majorities in the House and Senate.

Dying Former Congressman Barney Frank Tells Democrats Their Far-left Messaging Is Costing Them Voters

"Don't say socialism ever again. We need to get back to the basics," then-Rep. Abigail Spanberger, D-Va., said at the time.

But Tlaib, along with other progressives in the party, pushed back, arguing that their platforms would set the future tone of the party. In a widely circulated memo on Nov. 10, 2020, they made the case that progressives would appeal to an expanded voter base.

"We need a new generation of leadership grounded in a multiracial, working-class experience and background," the memo urged.

"As we speak, congressional Democrats are debating why they underperformed and some have been quick to blame progressives. There is no denying Republicans levied salient rhetorical attacks against Democrats, but these will continue to happen as they do every cycle."

Tlaib, in comments to Politico at the time, argued the platform would appeal to a kind of populist streak in the Democratic Party, similar to the populism she saw present in Trump's appeal among the GOP.

Far-left Surge: Mamdani-backed Candidates Oust Dem Establishment Incumbents

"If we truly want to unify our country, we have to really respect every single voice. We say that so willingly when we talk about Trump supporters, but we don't say that willingly for my Black and Brown neighbors and for LGBTQ neighbors or marginalized people," Tlaib said.

Having once again secured the Democratic nomination in 2026, Tlaib will advance to the general election on Nov. 3, 2026, where she is heavily favored to win. She last won re-election against Republican challenger James Hooper in a 69.7% to 25.4% victory in 2024.

Original article source: 'Squad' socialist scores re-election nod as radical wave continues to sweep party

title: Bypass will slash congestion, claims business case
description: Phase one of Hereford bypass is forecast to cut traffic by up to 25%.
fullText:
A business case for phase one of the Hereford bypass has claimed congestion in parts of the city could fall by up to 25%.

It also said journey times between the city centre and Rotherwas could reduce by an average of six-and-a-half-minutes.

Herefordshire Council decided to publish the full document ahead of work starting on the route, which will link the A49 and A465 south of the city.

Councillor Philip Price, cabinet member for transport and infrastructure, said: "One of the reasons we have produced a detailed business case is to demonstrate that the scheme represents good value for money."

About £45m has been put aside for the bypass, which will create an alternative route for vehicles to travel around the city.

The business case - which has been published by an infrastructure consultancy called AECOM - runs to 30 pages.

It forecasted that average daily traffic would fall by between 15% and 25% along Walnut Tree Avenue and the A465, both of which suffer regular hold-ups.

It also suggested a smaller drop in traffic of 7% along Holme Lacy Road, and listed "improved reliability of bus services" as one of the benefits.

Drivers would also benefit from reduced travel times between the A465 and Herefordshire Enterprise Zone, where 3,500 people work, of about six-and-a-half minutes.

The document also cited "quieter residential streets" as a benefit, with fewer drivers seeking to cut their journey times by using the well-known rat runs.

Price added: "Publishing the full business case is an important milestone in progressing the Hereford bypass.

"[It] sets out the benefits the scheme will bring, including improving connectivity, supporting businesses, unlocking growth and creating better places for people across Herefordshire.

"Delivering a scheme of this importance will require the support and involvement of the whole community.

"It represents an important first step towards a more connected and resilient transport network for Herefordshire."

The bypass has been divisive - residents have voiced concern over the cash-strapped council earmarking another £5m towards it, on top of the £40m that had already been committed.

The council is also in a legal standoff with a woman who is refusing to sell her land for phase one to start, due to an ancient tree in her back garden.

But bosses said they were confident work would still be able to start in December, with the first phase set to be complete in 2028.

Phase two, which would include a second river crossing over the River Wye to the west of the city, is subject to further funding and planning permission.

title: Wisconsin judge rules that paper absentee ballots violate rights of certain disabled people
description: Absentee voting in Wisconsin discriminates against disabled voters, a judge ruled Tuesday, siding with groups that are seeking to force election officials to allow for electronic casting of ballots.  ...
fullText:
MADISON, Wis. (AP) — Absentee voting in Wisconsin discriminates against disabled voters, a judge ruled Tuesday, siding with groups that are seeking to force election officials to allow for electronic casting of ballots.

But Dane County Circuit Judge Everett Mitchell stopped short of ordering electronic voting, setting up a trial on that issue later. It almost certainly will not be resolved before the November election.

Disability Rights Wisconsin, the League of Women Voters and four disabled voters brought the lawsuit in 2024. They argued that the lack of an electronic absentee voting option violated their right to independence and privacy and the protections of the Americans with Disabilities Act.

Mitchell issued a temporary injunction in 2024, saying that disabled voters should have the option to vote electronically. But an appeals court reversed that ruling, sending it back to the lower court, saying it was wrong to issue a temporary injunction that would have changed and "significantly disrupted the status quo."

The Republican-controlled Legislature is fighting the lawsuit.

Mitchell ruled on Tuesday that the state's absentee ballot program, which requires voters to complete and return a ballot on paper, denies disabled people "the equal opportunity to vote absentee privately and independently."

The judge declined to order elections officials to offer electronic ballots to qualified disabled voters, saying the parties still disputed whether that was a reasonable remedy. The judge noted that those included the difficulty of instituting such a program and the risks involved.

Under his previous ruling, made before more facts in the case were presented, Mitchell said that voters who self-certify that they can't read or mark a paper ballot without help would be eligible to request an electronic ballot.

Absentee ballots are currently emailed to military and overseas voters from Wisconsin.

Neither those who brought the lawsuit nor the Wisconsin Elections Commission had any estimates of how many disabled voters would request absentee ballots electronically.

Spokespeople for the elections commission and the Wisconsin Department of Justice, which represented the commission, did not immediately return messages seeking comment.

A hearing on the case is set for Aug. 12, where a potential trial date could be set.

title: Man gets third-degree burns from hot sand after using disposable beach BBQ
description: Sam Knight was left with severely blistered feet from hot sand after using a disposable barbecue.
fullText:
Warning: This article contains a distressing image

A man who suffered third-degree burns from hot sand after using a disposable barbecue on a beach has warned others to be aware of the dangers.

Sam Knight had been using it on Cefn Sidan Beach, Carmarthenshire, with his family and stepped on sand that was still hot.

The 27-year-old had to be carried off the beach after suffering badly blistered feet and needed weeks of treatment.

Experts at a burns centre say injuries such as this are becoming increasingly common and warned beachgoers to take precautions.

Knight told Radio Wales Breakfast he was not aware that sand could be a "real hazard".

He had used tongs to move the barbecue to one side and extinguished it, so he thought it was safe.

"When I returned to the area, I stepped on a boiling hot patch of sand, and had to be carried off the beach," he added.

Knight said he was taken to Neath Port Talbot Hospital where he was told he would need a burns specialist.

"I couldn't walk for a couple of weeks so I had to take a fortnight off work," he added.

David Fligelstone and Menna Davies are physiotherapists who work with the burns centre at Swansea Bay University Health Board.

Fligelstone said the number of incidents they are seeing is "going up year on year".

"The key thing is that people don't understand is that that sand stays hot for such a long time after a barbecue is moved," he said.

"When you look at the evidence it's always the sand that hasn't been cooled that ends up causing that injury."

Davies said injuries like this can be "quite painful" and need to be dressed for a "long period of time".

According to the NHS guidelines you should:

Hold the burn or scald under cool running water for 15 to 30 minutes, or until the pain feels better. If there's no running water available, you can use cool bottled water.

Remove any clothing or jewellery that's near the affected area – but do not remove anything that is stuck to the affected area.

When the burn or scald has cooled, lay cling film over it if you can. Do not wrap the cling film around it.

Following his recovery, Knight decided to conduct an experiment with two disposable barbecues.

He found that raising the barbecue from the sand kept it closer to the ambient temperature.

Swansea Bay Health Board recommended using stones, bricks or a dedicated stand to prevent heat transferring to the sand.

Used barbecues should also be disposed of by placing in a designated hot-ash bin or taken home.

The health board said all beach sand burns in children required urgent medical assessment.

title: Teachers need help with AI. A union is offering training – with $23m in funding from big tech
description:
Partnership between American Federation of Teachers, one of the largest labor unions in the US, and AI firms has stirred controversy
Darius Saczuk, a high school teacher, views artificial intelligence as his enemy. Earlier this year, he and several dozen New York City teachers spent the day inside a windowless conference room in downtown Manhattan to learn how to use AI and prevent students from outsourcing their thinking to it.
As Saczuk sees it, he needs to understand his enemy in order to beat it.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Partnership between American Federation of Teachers, one of the largest labor unions in the US, and AI firms has stirred controversy

Darius Saczuk, a high school teacher, views artificial intelligence as his enemy. Earlier this year, he and several dozen New York City teachers spent the day inside a windowless conference room in downtown Manhattan to learn how to use AI and prevent students from outsourcing their thinking to it.

As Saczuk sees it, he needs to understand his enemy in order to beat it.

“It’s killing our jobs, it’s changing our society, it’s replacing humans,” said Saczuk, who teaches English as a new language at Long Island City high school in Queens. “In order to retain my job, I need to know how to use AI because it’s not going away.”

So he turned to training offered by the American Federation of Teachers, one of the largest labor unions in the US with roughly 1.8 million members, at its new National Academy for AI Instruction. Last year, the academy began offering in-person and virtual AI training across the country. The goal is to train 400,000 educators over the span of five years, helping them understand AI’s benefits and potential harms and also shape how it’s used in the classroom.

Without guidance from their schools or districts, many teachers are left to figure out whether and how to use AI tools. Though the AFT’s $23m training initiative is one of the few structured programs for teachers, its funding, provided entirely by Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic, is stirring controversy. Supporters say the training is necessary for the future, but critics argue the academy pushes AI into classrooms, steering teachers toward tools that undermine students’ learning.

“It’s handing more political power over” to big tech, said Audrey Watters, author of Teaching Machines: The History of Personalized Learning. It’s really “dangerous” for educators to partner with companies that “seem opposed” to the goal of education, she said.

AI has become a ubiquitous force in classrooms, despite the lack of official guidance. More than half of polled teens say they use AI for help with schoolwork and nearly six in 10 think using AI to cheat is a regular occurrence at their schools, according to a Pew Research Center survey conducted last fall. Meanwhile only about four in 10 teachers say their schools offer professional development or training related to AI, according to a recent NPR/Ipsos poll. And about half of all teachers polled say their school hasn’t offered any guidance on AI, or they’re unclear on what it is.

Teaching educators about AI is a “moral imperative”, said Randi Weingarten, the AFT president. She argues that AI training empowers teachers to make informed decisions about how, when or whether to use AI in their instruction. And without outside funding, it was a choice between taking big yech’s money or doing nothing, she said.

“There was no fairy godmother philanthropist that was sprinkling millions of dollars on us to actually create a mechanism to educate,” Weingarten said. “I am not promoting the use of AI. Educators need to know the tool.”

For Microsoft, which is contributing the largest share of funding at $12.5m, the goal is to give educators a voice in shaping how AI products are used, said Justin Spelhaug, leader of Microsoft’s education, workforce and nonprofit programs.

“By partnering with teachers’ unions … we believe we can learn directly from teachers on what they want and need in their classroom,” he said in a statement.

But Watters asserts that AI’s presence in the classroom is not a foregone conclusion.

“The industry would very much like us to believe that it’s not going away,” Watters said. “But the future is unwritten.”

Tech company leaders have largely painted AI as beneficial to education, some even claiming AI could replace teachers. But experts say there’s still a lack of research proving whether AI actually improves learning outcomes.

In a 2024 blog post, Sam Altman, the OpenAI CEO, said he envisioned a future where “children will have virtual tutors”. AI could replicate some of the meaningful experiences teachers provide, such as making students feel understood and inspired, Greg Brockman, the OpenAI president, said in 2023 on the Possible podcast, hosted by Reid Hoffman, the LinkedIn co-founder, and Aria Finger, his chief of staff.

“Imagine if you could give that kind of teacher to every student 24/7 … for free,” Brockman said.

Microsoft believes “AI can help reduce administrative burdens, personalize learning and create more time for students”, Spelhaug said. “But there is no substitute for the role of a teacher.”

OpenAI, which pledged $10m to the academy, and Anthropic, which committed $500,000 to the first year, did not respond to a request for comment.

AI companies are already making their way into classrooms. Over the last two years, Miami-Dade county public schools, one of the largest US districts, began rolling out Google’s Gemini chatbot to teachers and high school students. Last fall, Microsoft announced AI tools for teachers at no additional cost for educational customers. And OpenAI and Anthropic offer K-12 teachers free use of versions of their chatbots designed for educators.

There’s been a longstanding playbook in which tech companies provide free training and resources to teachers in exchange for feedback and product advocacy, said Justin Reich, a Massachusetts Institute of Technology professor and author of Failure to Disrupt: Why Technology Alone Can’t Transform Education.

Google, for example, entrenched itself in schools by offering districts free or low-cost educational software for classroom laptops. It’s also built a corps of Google Certified Educators, teachers trained on the company’s software who promote it to their peers. Last year, Google introduced free Gemini certifications for K-12 teachers and students as young as 13. But the aim is profits, Reich said.

“Their goal is to get people to become lifelong consumers,” he said. Still, “there’s no evidence that the adoption of Google or Microsoft products lead to better outcomes, happier teachers, more efficient school systems or anything”.

The AFT’s new academy seems to echo Google’s approach, Watters said. By offering training through a labor union, viewed as a peer group, tech companies make their AI products seem more credible, she said.

“It feels very different to have your union say, ‘We’re offering a training,’ than it does to have a company say [it],” Watters said.

The concern is “understandable” though not accurate, Spelhaug said.

“This initiative was designed in response to a need our union partners and educators themselves identified,” he said. “Our role is to provide resources and expertise while respecting the independence of the AFT and the professional judgment of teachers.”

The AFT doesn’t allow companies to promote products during the sessions, Weingarten said. And while she doesn’t think “students have to use AI in schools”, she believes educators cannot ignore what’s already here.

In a May speech at the National Press Club, Weingarten called for a ban on student-facing AI in elementary schools and said the AFT is working with Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic on a “gold standard” for AI safety and privacy in schools. If the companies don’t deliver on the promise, the union will walk away from the funding, she added.

“They have agreed in concept,” she said. “But until the Is are dotted and the Ts are crossed, there’s no agreement.”

Microsoft didn’t share any details or timeline about new standards, but Spelhaug said the company shares the AFT’s goal.

There’s no established approach for training teachers on AI. The technology is simply too new. But the academy’s leaders hope to work with teachers to find ways to use the technology without compromising students’ cognitive development, independent thinking, data privacy and mental health.

“The sad thing is there is no map, and the terrain is changing every single day,” John Holleran, an AI academy trainer said to teachers assembled at a May session. “So, it’s going to be difficult for us to sort of figure out where we’re going.”

Demand for the academy’s training is strong. A May training sold out within hours, leaving about 150 people on the waitlist, according to staff. The session focused on two key points: AI can’t replace teachers. And it can’t be blindly trusted because it can be biased or hallucinate, meaning make things up.

For example, ChatGPT generated an image of a white man in a suit and tie when asked to show a successful person – a bias Holleran said teachers need to be aware of when creating prompts.

Several teachers at the training said AI is already helping them tackle classroom challenges.

Phillip Perry, who teaches ninth grade at Bronx High School for Law and Community Service, uses AI to design lessons for students with disabilities.

“Trying to differentiate instruction in a way that can completely target their learning needs has been a massive challenge,” Perry said. “Using AI is helpful in breaking down tasks to the smallest form to help build the students up as they go.”

Tanushree Sengupta, a math teacher at Hillcrest high school in Queens, uses AI to generate practice math problems and, eventually, to analyze student data and flag those needing extra support or a challenge. But she worries that the tech could be a crutch.

“I need to figure out ways where [students are] doing more thinking that they can actually show,” she said, adding that she signed up for the training in part to help students think for themselves.

To that end, AFT trainers advised teachers to redesign their curriculum to favor student-led discussions, journaling and thought exercises that require human judgement and reasoning.

The training filled a void, offering practical strategies for the classroom, said Perry and Sengupta, who were unaware of the academy’s funding prior to speaking to the Guardian.

“As long as what they’re providing is beneficial to the students and the teachers, then I don’t see an issue,” Perry said.

Saczuk, the teacher from Queens, considered the training “necessary”. Still, he left with more questions than answers.

“What is the role of the teacher?” he asked. “It’s a big question mark.”

title: ‘If we don’t fight back, we don’t have a future’: the journalist taking on the ‘tech fascists’ of Silicon Valley
description:

fullText:
As Elon Musk, Peter Thiel and their peers have grown richer and more influential, Gil Durán argues they have all but abandoned democracy – and found the perfect government to enable them

In April, Gil Durán was permanently banned from Elon Musk’s X for posting just two words. Durán was responding to a post from the tech company Palantir outlining its 22‑point “technological manifesto”, which praised American “hard power”, western culture and AI weapons, denounced inclusivity and called for compulsory national service. Durán responded: “TLDR: Fascism” (TLDR is short for “too long, didn’t read”).

Durán didn’t break any of X’s written rules, he points out over a video call from San Francisco – so much for Musk’s “free-speech absolutism”. His ban might just have had something to do with his preceding tweet, showing the cover of his new book, The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy. The book’s central argument is that big tech is no longer our friend, as many of its billionaire owners have seized economic and political control and are steering the fate of the planet towards their own bizarre, apocalyptic visions.

Fascism is no exaggeration, Durán asserts. He researched multiple definitions – by Umberto Eco, Robert Paxton, Jason Stanley – and decided that Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement ticks all the boxes. “It’s a cult of grievance that seeks to purge its enemies by demonising them through absurd and surreal propaganda that exploits fears over law and order and gender and sexuality in order to seize power and install a permanent hierarchy that fascists consider the moral order of the world and the universe. In addition, you also have this sort of nationalistic, militaristic vibe.”

In addition, Durán believes, “Silicon Valley has gone fascist because they have adopted an extreme ideology of tech supremacy.” While Maga promises a return to a mythical glorious past, he says, the “technofascists” are promising a mythical glorious future: “We’re going to be in the stars. We’re going to be in space. And all we need is to get rid of anybody who stands in our way as we seek to accelerate technology toward this speedy, violent, God-like transcendence that we will achieve if we can only burn enough energy and enough compute to bring our boom loop into existence.”

It sounds almost like a conspiracy theory, but Durán is not short of evidence. Musk making an apparent Nazi salute and describing empathy as “the fundamental weakness of western civilisation”. Palantir’s Peter Thiel writing in 2009 that “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible” and giving a lecture series suggesting Greta Thunberg could be the antichrist. Marc Andreessen, the CEO of the tech investment company Andreessen Horowitz, paraphrasing Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, the co-author of Mussolini’s Fascist Manifesto, in his “Techno-Optimist Manifesto”: “Technology must be a violent assault on the forces of the unknown, to force them to bow before man.”

Durán, a journalist and former political adviser, lays out the narrative in exacting detail, outlining the connections between these men (and it is all men) and the origins of their often deeply weird beliefs, many of which view everyone outside their circle or opposed to their agenda as expendable.

Unpacking all their overlapping philosophies would take some time, but TLDR: “It’s the idea that what matters more is the billions or trillions of people yet unborn in the future. And the only way they’re going to get to be born is if this elite group of white tech figures and gazillionaires makes the right decisions to make the human race transhuman and multiplanetary through AI and technology,” says Durán. “By becoming a billionaire, they all have this idea that they’re superior to everyone else. They are susceptible to this kind of thinking.”

Durán, 50, is almost the opposite: the son of working-class Mexican immigrants in California. He was the first in his family to go to college, having grown up in relative poverty: “It made me tough and gave me an unyielding loyalty to regular people over the many rich and powerful people I’ve spent a lot of my time around.”

Durán’s book traces the roots of this movement to two important sources. One is the 1997 book The Sovereign Individual, written by the American investor James Dale Davidson and William Rees-Mogg, the former Times editor and BBC grandee (and father of Jacob). Their book prophesied how digital tools such as the internet and cryptocurrency would pave the way for a privatised, corporatised, unregulated, post-democratic future ruled by rich, powerful, unaccountable individuals. Two decades later, this led to the idea of “network states” – digital realms beyond the jurisdiction of nation states – as popularised by Balaji Srinivasan, a former partner at Andreessen Horowitz.

The other source is Curtis Yarvin, a former software developer and armchair philosopher with a penchant for psychedelics, sometimes referred to as the godfather of the “dark enlightenment”. In pseudonymous blogs in the late 2000s, Yarvin outlined a worldview in which liberal democracy had failed to deliver progress, partly because institutions such as education and the media had been captured by what he called “the Cathedral”.

His proposed solution was a mass firing of government employees (he coined the acronym “Rage”, “retire all government employees”) and the installation of a “national CEO, [or] what’s called a dictator”. Yarvin also mused about a “humane alternative to genocide” to deal with unproductive citizens and has had to deny accusations that he is a white supremacist or supports racist ideologies. Scratch the surface, Durán suggests, and Yarvin’s ideas have much in common with Nazi ideologies, “but updated as rightwing dogma for the blogging age”.

Both of these sources might have languished in obscurity had it not been for Thiel, the man at the heart of Silicon Valley’s rightward lurch. He has amassed enormous wealth through a series of investments in tech startups – first PayPal, then Facebook, Spotify, LinkedIn, Palantir and OpenAI, among others. He was the first major tech figure to back Donald Trump, in July 2016, and persuaded others to follow, including Andreessen, who said he spent half his time at Mar-a-Lago in the month after Trump won the 2024 election.

Thiel liked The Sovereign Individual so much that he wrote a new introduction when it was reprinted in 2020. He has also made steps to found his own network state – first via the ill-fated “seasteading” movement (establishing floating countries in international waters) then via Próspera, a “special economic zone” on an island in Honduras. Incorporated in 2017 with permission from the Honduran government and reportedly co-funded by Srinivasan, Andreessen and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Próspera has sought to attract digital startups with loose regulations (appealing to longevity researchers), low taxes and a crypto-friendly economy.

Other similar projects have sprung up. In 2021, the president of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, hailed the mooted creation of a “Bitcoin City”. In 2023, Trump announced plans to build 10 “Freedom Cities” on government land across the US, with input from Próspera representatives. In 2024, Srinivasan founded a “Network School” in Johor, Malaysia.

Thiel also began to absorb Yarvin’s theories about how the political order was preventing progress. In the 2009 essay in which Thiel declared the incompatibility of freedom and democracy, he also said “the vast increase in welfare beneficiaries and the extension of the franchise to women” made capitalist democracy impossible, which did not win him many mainstream supporters. But Yarvin backed up Thiel and the two became friends and allies. “While The Sovereign Individual provided the foundation for the billionaire’s political vision, Yarvin created a blueprint for turning that vision into reality,” Durán writes.

Thiel was instrumental in injecting these ideas, and people, into the US government – not least JD Vance, whom Durán describes as “almost entirely a creation of Peter Thiel”. It was Thiel who set up Vance as a venture capitalist, giving him a role at his firm Mithril Capital, then investing in Vance’s own fund, Narya Capital (Tolkien-derived names are a theme with these people). It was Thiel who backed Vance’s move into politics, where he went from condemning Trump as “America’s Hitler” to supporting him and parroting Yarvin’s ideas. “I think that what Trump should do, if I was giving him one piece of advice: fire every single mid-level bureaucrat, every civil servant in the administrative state, replace them with our people,” Vance told the podcaster Jack Murphy in 2021.

Durán had observed this Silicon Valley takeover developing and began writing about it in 2024. “I thought this would be a problem in five to 10 years, but when JD Vance got on the ticket, it suddenly took on a new urgency,” he says. Now, it almost feels too late. In 2025, Bloomberg reported that at least 16 men connected to Thiel and his companies occupied positions of power in the Trump administration, including David Sacks, who is now a special adviser for AI and crypto. Musk’s Doge has swung its chainsaw at the government, crypto and AI regulation has all but disappeared, the Trump family are now billionaires and the tech oligarchs have become the Republicans’ largest donors.

At the same time, they have become substantial beneficiaries of the very government they once sought to dismantle. Palantir has an estimated $13.7bn in US government contracts; last year, its stock price rose more than 90% in six months. Andreessen is backing dozens of defence companies scooping up government contracts and recently joined the Pentagon’s advisory board. Last week, Musk’s SpaceX received a $1.6bn contract to supply rockets to the US Space Force – on the same day he pledged at least $100m to help Republicans in November’s midterm elections.

“It’s a severe cautionary tale about the hazards of privatisation,” says Durán. “The government created these men, especially Elon Musk. And now these welfare kings want to pull up the ladder, want to destroy the very system that made them. This is a massive failure by the US intelligence apparatus – to not see this threat forming from the inside.”

Durán, who worked in communications for Kamala Harris when she was California’s attorney general, as well as for the late Democratic senator Dianne Feinstein, blames the Democrats as much as the Republicans. “They have failed tremendously to stand up to billionaire power because the only people as addicted to billionaire money in American politics as the Republicans are the Democrats,” he says.

He singles out the California governor, Gavin Newsom, as a prime example of a “Silicon Valley Democrat”: “You don’t see him criticising these guys. He only goes after Trump, Trump, Trump and Vance, Vance, Vance … You want some viral content? Why don’t you go off on Peter Thiel’s weird antichrist obsession?” Even if the Democrats take control after the midterms or the 2028 presidential election, Durán is worried that “these tech fascists will win … because Democrats will not hold them accountable”.

On the plus side, the Silicon Valley takeover has not been going that well lately. Network states around the world are losing ground. In 2021, Próspera’s special economic status was repealed by the new president, Xiomara Castro (it is suing the Honduran government for $10.8bn). Two weeks ago, Srinivasan’s Network School was ordered to close (Srinivasan says he is moving it to Kazakhstan). Trump’s Freedom Cities remain unbuilt.

One saving grace, says Durán, is that “a lot of these people don’t really have a great grasp of on-the-ground realities”. Nobody really wants to live in a soulless network state, he says: “Why would you be in Kazakhstan instead of San Francisco, which is the global capital of tech?” On the other hand, he points out, the tech billionaires have effectively turned the US into a de facto network state.

But they may well have overplayed their hand. “Silicon Valley oligarchs are really vulnerable right now,” says Durán. “People don’t like them. People are starting to rise up against data centres and this vision of an AI apocalypse that kills all the jobs and potentially kills all of humanity. You’re scaring the hell out of people and now they don’t like you. Into that could step a politician to take advantage of that trend and come up with a message that speaks to the concerns of people and against the dark fantasies of the oligarchs.”

The question now, he says, “is how we turn the momentum in our favour and against the billionaires. Because they have a plan to win. They think they’re going to succeed.” This could be a radicalising moment: “In fighting against billionaire power, we find the key to all of our problems. Every moment is an important opportunity to wake people up and to start to fight back.”

If not, he says, we’ll find ourselves in a situation where “we don’t have democracy, we don’t have an economy and we don’t have a future. If that doesn’t radicalise people, then we deserve what we’re going to get.”

The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy is published on 18 August (Simon & Schuster, £25). To support the Guardian, buy a copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply

description:

fullText:
AI Security Institute says models by OpenAI and Anthropic went rogue during a cybersecurity test and showed a new type of risk

Advanced AI models developed by OpenAI and Anthropic went rogue during a cybersecurity test and showed a new type of risk posed by the technology, according to the UK’s AI Security Institute.

AISI described the actions carried out by the agents – the term for AI systems that can perform tasks without human help – as a “serious incident”. In one example, an agent powered by Anthropic’s Mythos model sent targeted emails to people.

AISI said the rogue behaviour was carried out by agents powered by two models – Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol.

AISI said it detected unusual activity during a routine cybersecurity test for AI models on 28 July. It found that some of the agents had engaged in “sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations”. It took an hour to contain the incident.

In the most serious case, an agent powered by Mythos tried to insert malicious code into an open-source software project on GitHub, a platform used by software developers. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent then created fake online identities based on real people and used them to press the project’s overseer into accepting the code. These attempts were blocked by a human developer.

AISI said the agent used techniques commonly associated with real-world hackers. It sent emails to specifically chosen individuals – a technique known as “spear-phishing” – that attempted to manipulate the recipient. Some of the messages contained harmful software.

AISI said no harm was caused but the agents’ actions were unprecedented.

“This is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real world,” said AISI in a blogpost.

The incident followed recent similar episodes at OpenAI and Anthropic. In July, OpenAI said an agent powered by its models had hacked an AI startup during a test, and days later Anthropic said its Claude model had hacked three organisations during an evaluation.

AISI said the incident, taken alongside similar occurrences at OpenAI and Anthropic, represented a “shift in the risk landscape”. This was not an example of deliberate misuse of publicly available models, AISI said, but showed models in a research environment taking unintended action “beyond their authorised scope”.

AISI said 17 of the 19 cases of rogue behaviour that occurred during the evaluation were carried out by Mythos and two by Sol.

AISI said this was not a case of a model escaping its “sandbox”, or secure testing environment. The institute said it had intentionally permitted internet access and disabled filters within the models that blocked dangerous behaviour. The models are not publicly available in those operating conditions and there is no sign of such behaviour happening outside tests, AISI said.

The incident should be interpreted with “caution and nuance”, AISI said, but the signs of deceptive behaviour were “to an extent and severity we did not anticipate”. It was a small number of events that occurred under specific conditions, AISI added, but it had not happened before.

“What we can say is that the behaviour was possible, sustained and new. That alone warrants attention,” AISI said.

AISI admitted it was not actively monitoring the agents’ behaviour during the evaluation. It said it was putting tighter controls on internet access in tests as a result of the incident, introducing constant monitoring of tests and reassessing its design of tests. It said evaluations should assume a model would attempt to act beyond its remit.

The UK’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, said it was “absolutely vital” that the UK had a world-leading AI safety organisation. “Identifying new behaviour like this and sharing our findings, so we can tackle it, is exactly what AISI was set up to do,” he said.

OpenAI said the testing occurred during “conditions that do not reflect ordinary use”. An OpenAI spokesperson said: “We’ll continue working with evaluators and other stakeholders across the industry to strengthen shared practices for conducting evaluations safely as models become more capable.”

Anthropic said the incident “underscores the need for a broader conversation about how to safely evaluate increasingly capable AI agents” and it would continue to work with AISI on evaluating what happened.

Barcelona passed on the chance to sign Chelsea ace to prioritize Gordon and Alvarez – report
description: Barcelona have spent the summer transfer window signing Anthony Gordon from Newcastle United and Karim Adeyemi from Borussia Dortmund.They have also been very keen on signing Julian Alvarez from Atlet...
fullText:
Barcelona have spent the summer transfer window signing Anthony Gordon from Newcastle United and Karim Adeyemi from Borussia Dortmund.

They have also been very keen on signing Julian Alvarez from Atletico Madrid, with the Argentine emerging as Deco and Hansi Flick's dream striker target.

Barça have still not given up hope of signing the 26-year-old striker, with Deco in Madrid to hold talks with the player's camp and devise a strategy.

Now, according to journalist Joaquim Piera on SPORT, Barcelona had a genuine opportunity to sign Joao Pedro before Chelsea closed the door on a possible summer departure.

The Catalan club instead directed their resources towards Anthony Gordon and continued working on a move for Julian Alvarez.

Barcelona could have signed Joao Pedro in June. (Photo by Stuart C. Wilson/Getty Images for AELTC, Wimbledon)

Chelsea were prepared to negotiate in June, with a deal potentially possible for around €80 million plus €20 million in variables.

However, Deco prioritised strengthening the left wing after Raphinha's injury problems created uncertainty around the position.

Barcelona eventually spent €80 million on Gordon, who is expected to compete with the Brazilian rather than simply replace Marcus Rashford in the squad.

Gordon's ability to operate as a false nine also gave Hansi Flick another tactical option. Even so, he is not a natural long-term successor to Robert Lewandowski.

Barça had identified Alvarez as their priority striker option, but it is well into August and the club have still not signed the Argentine attacker.

Alvarez remains the priority target. (Photo by Florencia Tan Jun/Getty Images)

Meanwhile, Joao Pedro is close to signing an improved contract at Chelsea set to run until 2033. Arsenal also explored a transfer for the Brazilian, but the Blues did not want to strengthen a direct London rival.

For Barcelona, they made a calculated gamble by not signing the Chelsea striker, and that does not seem to have panned out well so far.

However, if the club manage to go on and sign Alvarez, the decision not to pursue a move for Joao Pedro will look smart in hindsight.

The next few weeks will determine whether Barça made a smart decision by not signing Joao Pedro or whether it will go down as a missed opportunity.

fullText:
According to meczyki.pl, Borussia Dortmund's chief scout Bastian Schulz was conducting some research in the Polish topflight last week.

Schulz attended Legia Warsaw's 3-1 victory over Zagłębie Lubin on Sunday to observe attacking midfielder Marcel Regula.

Regula's employer confirmed to the Polish sports portal that the Westphalian giants are intrigued by the 19-year-old talent.

Meanwhile, Sky Germany also reported several days ago that fellow Bundesliga side 1.FC Köln were also keen to sign the youngster.

It's clear that if Borussia Dortmund goes ahead with the deal for the midfielder, Köln won't be able to compete financially.

However, the Cathedral City club might be able to offer the young professional more playing time compared to a competitive BVB squad.

Besides Dortmund and Effzeh, a number of other clubs from around the European continent have Regula on their radar.

title: Carlos Alcaraz’s Cincinnati withdrawal confirmed as injury concerns grow ahead of US Open
description: The No. 2 ranked men’s tennis star will not be participating in the Cincinnati Open due to a wrist injury that is set to keep him out.
fullText:
The No. 2 ranked men's tennis star will not be participating in the Cincinnati Open due to a wrist injury that is set to keep him out.

Carlos Alcaraz is arguably the biggest star in tennis at the moment. The Spaniard is ranked No. 2 in the ATP rankings, behind reigning Wimbledon champion Jannik Sinner.

Alcaraz and Sinner have quickly established themselves as the main men in the current scene. However, they haven't clashed at the highest level in a while, with Carlos missing both the French Open and Wimbledon.

The 23-year-old has spent most of 2026 recovering from a wrist injury. And just as he was set to make his return to ramp up ahead of the US Open, Alcaraz has suffered another setback.

One of the oldest tennis tournaments in the United States, the Cincinnati Open is generally a great precursor for the US Open, which is set to follow later in August.

For Alcaraz, it would have been an excellent launching pad as he makes his return from injury. However, it seems that won't be happening this year.

"Carlos Alcaraz has withdrawn from the Cincinnati Open," the tournament's official handle announced on X. "Wishing all the best to our 2025 champion in his recovery process. Can't wait to welcome you next year!

Alcaraz won the competition last year, and indeed, went on to win the US Open as well, defeating Sinner in four sets in the final.

With the Spaniard unable to participate, fans are worrying this will lead to him being unable to defend yet another major title. Hopefully, Alcaraz will still be able to make it back in time for the big one.

title: ‘LeBron, do you have any desire to be a woman?’: Donald Trump reveals plans as WNBA coach
description: Donald Trump has felt strongly about basketball as of late. The President recently weighed in on one of the longest-lasting debates going on in sports circles: who the greatest basketball player of all time is. While it’s widely viewed as a two-horse race between Michael Jordan and LeBron James, Trump made it clear that for…
fullText:
Donald Trump has felt strongly about basketball as of late. The President recently weighed in on one of the longest-lasting debates going on in sports circles: who the greatest basketball player of all time is. While it's widely viewed as a two-horse race between Michael Jordan and LeBron James, Trump made it clear that for him, it's a fairly easy choice.

"Well, Michael Jordan is a guy that's a friend of mine. He's a really good guy," Trump said during a press conference following James' decision to sign with the Philadelphia 76ers for his 24th season in the NBA. "And I think LeBron… Maybe he's a racist, but maybe he doesn't like Trump. I don't know. I only like people that like me, so I would say Michael Jordan all the way."

The NBA isn't the only basketball league the President has been following, either. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt revealed that the President has been following the controversy surrounding WNBA guard Sophie Cunningham of the Indiana Fever, who sparked debate when she said in a profile that she thinks it's important to keep transgender girls from competing in the same sports as other girls.

"I don't believe he (President Trump) has reached out to her. I know he is following the story. As you know, this is something the president feels strongly about as well, and the American people do, too: that men should not be playing in women's sports," Leavitt said.

"It's completely ludicrous that anyone could support that. It's even more ludicrous you have Sophie Cunningham, a female athlete herself, very accomplished in her own right, coming forth and speaking that truth that men shouldn't play in women's sports — we want to protect women and girls — and the backlash she is receiving from Democrats and left-wing fingers across the country is astonishing. They are clearly very out of touch with the American public on this issue."

Now, the President has linked his James-Jordan feelings and his take on trans athletes in the WNBA.

"I'd be the greatest women's basketball coach in history because I don't like LeBron James," Trump said in a public address, "I like Michael Jordan much better. But I'd go up to LeBron James.

“I’d be the greatest women’s basketball coach in history. I don’t like LeBron James, I like Michael Jordan much better. But, I’d go up to LeBron James…I’d say, ‘LeBron, did you ever have any desire to be a woman? Because what I’d love you to do is star on my team.” pic.twitter.com/xU5lt6hPeH

"It doesn't matter, I'd say, 'LeBron, did you ever have any desire to be a woman? Because what I'd love you to do is star on my team that I'm building up.' I will have the greatest team in history. They'll never lose. Nobody will come within 70 points of this team. Now, we have to change that, and we have to make it okay to talk about it."

It's an odd thing to say considering that the WNBA doesn't have a single transgender player in it, and no transgender athletes are dominating at the highest levels of college basketball either. The one transgender female basketball player that anti-trans advocates have used as an example recently, Julien Tetart, hasn't even reached the highest level of professional basketball in France

The post 'LeBron, do you have any desire to be a woman?': Donald Trump reveals plans as WNBA coach appeared first on The Comeback: Today's Top Sports Stories & Reactions.

title: Luis likes Ipswich's long-term plan
description: Ipswich Town have completed the signing of Florentino Luís from Burnley, with the midfielder stating the club's long-term thinking was key in attracting him.  The 26-year-old - who already offers Premier League experience - has signed a five-year deal at Portman Road, joining for an undisclosed fee.  "It feels brilliant to be a part of this club," Florentino said.
fullText:
Ipswich Town have completed the signing of Florentino Luís from Burnley, with the midfielder stating the club's long-term thinking was key in attracting him.

The 26-year-old - who already offers Premier League experience - has signed a five-year deal at Portman Road, joining for an undisclosed fee.

"It feels brilliant to be a part of this club," Florentino said.

"I think I will be very happy here. I like how the club sees the future and there are a lot of good players here. How the club is thinking to the long-term is one of the main reasons I came here.

"I can bring experience and balance to the team, between defence and attack, and I like to bring the connection.

"Now I have signed I can't wait to meet my teammates and the fans and get started with the team."

Luis made close to 200 appearances for Benfica before joining Burnley and on bolstering his midfield, Ipswich boss Gary O'Neil said: "We are delighted to have added Florentino to the group.

"He is a player who brings experience of playing in the Premier League as well as other major competitions in Europe, including the Champions League, and makes us stronger in central midfield.

"He brings quality off the ball, as well as on it, and we look forward to him joining up with the squad."

title: Browns’ Shedeur Sanders ranked as the worst veteran QB in the NFL; key reasons revealed
description: Cleveland Browns’ presumed QB1 Shedeur Sanders was ranked 35th out of the 35 eligible veteran QBs coming into the 2026-27 NFL season. Sanders had to fight his way to earn a starting role as the Browns’ QB over Dillon Gabriel last season, with this season’s battle also including veteran DeShaun Watson.
fullText:
Cleveland Browns' presumed QB1 Shedeur Sanders was ranked 35th out of the 35 eligible veteran QBs coming into the 2026-27 NFL season.

Sanders had to fight his way to earn a starting role as the Browns' QB over Dillon Gabriel last season, with this season's battle also including veteran DeShaun Watson.

Unfortunately, Sanders isn't going to enter next season as a rated QB, with executives and coaches clearly carrying a low opinion of the 24-year-old.

The Athletic's tier list survey of all 35 eligible veteran QBs saw Sanders rank dead-last, with some scathing comments from the respondents.

"He's inaccurate at all three levels," an exec said. "I can't tell if he is going to get better, but there's a huge gap between him and competent QB play."

"He's not an on-time player, can't really read through the coverages, is a little bit heavy-footed," one coordinator said. "He is thicker and harder to tackle than expected, but you shouldn't lose to him."

"I'd sleep like a baby if I got to play him every week," one defensive coordinator said.

While some recognized that Sanders could have upside under new head coach Todd Monken, they believe his existing performances rank him firmly as the worst of the bunch.

Sanders went 3-4 as a starter at the end of the season, going 120/212 on passes with a 56.6% completion and a below-average 68.1 passer rating.

Sanders' rival for the Browns' QB1 spot, Watson, ranked 31st in the same list. Sanders ranked behind quarterbacks like Minnesota Vikings' under-pressure J.J. McCarthy.

The upside is that Sanders literally has no other place to go but up heading into next season. He is getting most of the QB1 reps during the Browns' training camp.

Shedeur took all the first team reps during day six of Browns training camp, going 21/25 while Watson went 5/11.

It does look like the Browns will take the developmental risk of starting Sanders and having a veteran backup like Watson step in if Sanders isn't up to the task.

Dillon Gabriel will also factor in if neither of the QBs ahead of him can secure their spot.

The Browns haven't confirmed who their QB1 for the season will be, but all indicators point to Sanders right now.
